BUS-01.old: Governance tells you who has authority to decide what. The uploaded Business Environment notes use the flow Problem → Assess → Check → Owner → Act → Escalate.
BUS-01.summary: Governance is the set of rules for who is allowed to decide what. You care because many big decisions belong to the sponsor or a committee, not to you.
BUS-01.example: A vendor offers Maria a cheaper platform that would change the project's direction. She likes it, but that choice belongs to the steering committee. She studies the impact, prepares options, and takes them to the committee.
dos: Assess the problem before you do anything else
Check who owns the decision
Decide yourself when it sits inside your authority
Escalate with options when it is above your authority
donts: Do not make a major strategic decision alone.
Do not skip the approval path because the matter is urgent.
Do not escalate before you have analyzed the problem.
Do not push every small decision up to the sponsor.
BUS-01.rule: Problem → Assess → Check authority → Owner → Act → Escalate if needed
BUS-01.examCue: When a question says 'steering committee', 'approval' or 'decision owner', think: who has the authority? Assess first, then take it to that owner.

BUS-02.old: Compliance material treats laws, regulations, safety, audit, policy, and mandatory requirements as non-optional constraints that cannot simply be traded away for schedule or cost.
BUS-02.summary: Compliance means following the laws, regulations, safety rules and company policies that apply to your project. They are must-do items, so you cannot trade them away to save time or money.
BUS-02.example: Halfway through a clinic app build, Raj learns of a new patient privacy law. He checks what it requires, asks the legal team, and raises a change to add the needed work. He records what was done.
dos: Identify the rule and assess its impact on the project
Consult legal, safety or compliance experts
Update the plan or backlog through the proper process
Document the fix and prevent it happening again
donts: Do not ignore a new rule because scope is already baselined.
Do not pick speed or savings over legal or safety requirements.
Do not treat a mandatory control as something to negotiate.
Do not fix a gap quietly and leave no record.
BUS-02.rule: Identify → Assess → Consult → Update → Implement → Document
BUS-02.examCue: When a question says 'regulation', 'audit' or 'mandatory', think compliance: it is not optional. Assess the impact, consult the expert, then follow the change process.

BUS-03.old: The Business Environment notes explicitly separate organizational change from project change: organizational change is about people adopting a new behavior/capability, not just baseline control.
BUS-03.summary: Organizational change is about people starting to work in a new way. Your project only pays off when people actually use what you delivered, so adoption is part of your job.
BUS-03.example: A hospital launches a new scheduling system, but nurses keep using paper. Ana sits with them and learns the screens feel slow and confusing. She arranges short training, shares why the change helps, and checks usage weekly.
dos: Find out why people are resisting
Engage the people affected early
Explain the reasons and the benefits
Train users, then reinforce and measure adoption
donts: Do not treat resistance as bad behavior to punish.
Do not answer a people-adoption problem with a change request.
Do not assume going live means people are using it.
Do not escalate before you understand the resistance.
BUS-03.examCue: When a question says 'resistance', 'adoption' or 'users are not using it', think people change: understand why first, then engage, communicate and train.

BUS-04.old: The value materials emphasize Deliverable → Outcome → Benefit → Value and warn that completed scope is not the same as realized business value.
BUS-04.summary: A benefit is the measurable gain the organization gets from what you built. Finishing the work is not the win; the win is the result it creates, so you plan how to measure it.
BUS-04.example: Leo's team delivers a self-service portal on time. Three months later, call volume has not dropped, which was the whole point. Leo reviews the usage numbers with the operations owner and they agree actions to raise adoption.
dos: Ask what result the project was meant to create
Define how each benefit will be measured
Name an owner to track benefits after handoff
Use feedback and outcome numbers to recheck value
donts: Do not assume on time and on budget means success.
Do not treat handoff as the end of value.
Do not use ROI as the only measure of value.
Do not call a finished deliverable a benefit.
BUS-04.examCue: When a question says 'delivered but not used', 'outcome' or 'success criteria', think value: was the intended benefit measured and who owns it now?

BUS-05.old: Foundations and value-delivery material distinguish business need, business case, project delivery, benefits, and strategic value.
BUS-05.summary: The business need is the problem or opportunity; the business case explains why paying for the project is worth it. You care because a project must keep fitting the organization's goals.
BUS-05.example: A retailer approved a store-kiosk project last year. Now the company decides to move sales online. Priya does not keep building out of habit. She reviews the business case with the sponsor to see if the project still makes sense.
dos: Know the business need behind your project
Keep the project tied to the organization's strategy
Recheck the business case when conditions change a lot
Take the findings to the sponsor for a decision
donts: Do not continue only because the project was approved once.
Do not confuse finishing the work with creating strategic value.
Do not select projects using one number alone.
Do not cancel or redirect the project on your own.
BUS-05.rule: Business Need → Business Case → Project → Benefits → Value
BUS-05.examCue: When a question says 'strategy changed', 'new competitor' or 'market shift', think: reassess the business case with the sponsor before continuing.

BUS-06.old: The Business Environment material frames AI as decision support with human accountability and sustainability as environmental + social + economic lifecycle thinking.
BUS-06.summary: Responsible AI means using AI as a helper while a human stays accountable for the decision. Sustainability means weighing environmental, social and economic effects over the whole life of the product.
BUS-06.example: An AI tool gives Sam a schedule forecast that looks too good. He checks the data it used, finds missing tasks, and corrects it before reporting. He also keeps client names out of the tool because it is not approved.
dos: Check that the tool and the data are approved
Validate AI output before acting on it
Keep a human accountable for the final decision
Compare options by full lifecycle impact, not price alone
donts: Do not treat AI output as the final answer.
Do not put sensitive data into an unapproved AI tool.
Do not choose the cheapest or fastest option without checking long-term impact.
Do not let AI make governance decisions.
BUS-06.rule: AI: Protect data → Validate output → Human decides. Sustainability: think long term.
BUS-06.examCue: When a question says 'AI recommends', 'bias' or 'privacy', think validate, then a human decides. 'Lifecycle' or 'environmental' means balance long-term impact.

BUS-07.old: The Finance and Business Environment formula notes frame formulas as decision support: calculate, interpret, validate, decide.
BUS-07.summary: Finance measures such as ROI, NPV and payback help compare projects by the money they return. You care because the numbers support the decision, but they do not make it for you.
BUS-07.example: Two projects compete for funding. Project A has the higher NPV (value in today's money) but breaks a new regulation. Nina reports both numbers, flags the compliance problem, and recommends Project B to the selection committee.
dos: Calculate the measure the question asks for
Interpret what the number means for the business
Check the result against strategy, risk and compliance
Look at total cost of ownership, not purchase price
donts: Do not pick the highest number while ignoring compliance or strategy.
Do not keep going because of money already spent (sunk cost).
Do not choose the lowest purchase price over lifecycle value.
Do not confuse opportunity cost with sunk cost.
BUS-07.examCue: When a question says 'NPV', 'payback' or 'already spent', think: higher NPV, BCR and IRR are better, shorter payback is better, ignore sunk cost.

BUS-08.old: Foundations material distinguishes temporary project work from ongoing operations and separates project outcomes, program benefits, and portfolio strategy.
BUS-08.summary: A project is temporary and creates something unique. A program groups related projects, a portfolio groups work chosen for strategy, and operations is the ongoing daily work that runs the business.
BUS-08.example: A bank builds a mobile app (a project). The app, a new website and staff training are managed together as a digital program. Once live, the support desk answering customers every day is operations.
dos: Ask what the scenario is mainly focused on
Link a single unique result to a project
Link shared benefits across related projects to a program
Link choosing and prioritizing work to the portfolio
donts: Do not assume a long project is not temporary.
Do not treat a program as one large project.
Do not assume everything in a portfolio must be related.
Do not manage ongoing operations as a project.
BUS-08.rule: Project → Outcome | Program → Benefits | Portfolio → Strategy | Operations → Run business
BUS-08.examCue: When a question says 'related projects' think program; 'strategic alignment' or 'prioritize investments' think portfolio; 'ongoing' or 'repetitive' think operations.

PEO-01.old: Lead by enabling the team rather than controlling every task. The uploaded People notes emphasize coaching, removing blockers, empowering the team, protecting focus, active listening, and adapting leadership to the situation.
PEO-01.summary: Servant leadership means you lead by helping the team succeed instead of controlling every task. You care because the exam almost always prefers coaching and removing obstacles over giving orders.
PEO-01.example: A developer tells Grace she has waited four days for a test server. Grace does not tell her to work harder. She listens, calls the infrastructure lead, gets the server released, and checks back the next day.
dos: Listen to understand what the person needs
Coach and mentor the team
Remove obstacles that block the work
Let the team make decisions about its own work
donts: Do not use command-and-control with a capable team.
Do not escalate a team issue before talking with the people involved.
Do not solve every problem yourself; help the team solve it.
Do not micromanage tasks.
PEO-01.examCue: When a question says 'blocker', 'impediment' or 'self-organizing team', think servant leader: listen, coach, and remove the obstacle before escalating.

PEO-02.old: The uploaded leadership material presents the Thomas-Kilmann modes and frames collaborate/problem solve as the generally preferred win-win approach, while force/direct is reserved for urgent or non-negotiable contexts.
PEO-02.summary: Conflict is a normal part of teamwork, and there are five common ways to handle it. You care because the exam usually wants you to find the real cause and solve it together.
PEO-02.example: Two engineers argue over a design in every meeting. Omar meets them, listens to both, and learns each is protecting a different deadline. Together they agree a design that meets both dates, and Omar follows up a week later.
dos: Listen to each side first
Find the real cause behind the disagreement
Collaborate to reach a solution that works for both
Agree actions and follow up
donts: Do not treat compromise as the same as collaboration.
Do not blame personality before checking schedule, priorities and resources.
Do not escalate before the people involved try to resolve it.
Do not force a decision unless it is urgent or safety-critical.
PEO-02.examCue: When a question says 'disagreement' or 'two team members argue', think collaborate / problem solve. 'Both give something up' means compromise.

PEO-03.old: Team development is presented as Forming → Storming → Norming → Performing → Adjourning. Storming is normal, teams can regress, and leadership should change as the team matures.
PEO-03.summary: Tuckman's model describes five stages every team goes through, from first meeting to finishing. You care because the right leadership style depends on the stage your team is in.
PEO-03.example: Three weeks into a new project, Dana's team is arguing about who does what. She recognizes this as Storming, which is normal. She helps them agree ground rules and clear roles instead of replacing anyone.
dos: Identify which stage the team is in
Give clear direction to a brand-new team
Coach the team through conflict and set ground rules
Delegate more as the team matures
donts: Do not try to skip Storming.
Do not replace people when the conflict is normal team growth.
Do not use the same leadership style at every stage.
Do not forget a new member can move the team back a stage.
PEO-03.examCue: When a question says 'new team', 'new member joined' or 'arguing over roles', think Forming/Storming: coach and set ground rules; do not replace anyone yet.

PEO-04.old: The People notes cover Maslow, Herzberg, McGregor X/Y, McClelland, Vroom, Ouchi, and situational leadership. The goal is recognizing what motivates behavior rather than memorizing names alone.
PEO-04.summary: Motivation theories explain what makes people want to do good work. You care because the right response depends on what the person actually needs, and that is often not money.
PEO-04.example: Ken, a strong analyst, has become quiet and slow. Sara asks what has changed and learns he feels his work goes unnoticed. She gives him ownership of a visible report and recognizes his results in the team meeting.
dos: Find the need behind the behavior
Fix basic issues such as pay and conditions first
Use recognition, growth and responsibility to motivate
Match your approach to the person
donts: Do not use more pay as the answer to every motivation problem.
Do not assume everyone is motivated by the same thing.
Do not treat the models as rigid formulas.
Do not confuse hygiene factors with motivators.
PEO-04.rule: Need → Motivation signal → Right leadership response
PEO-04.examCue: When a question says 'salary and conditions' think Herzberg hygiene; 'recognition' or 'growth' think motivators; 'achievement, affiliation, power' think McClelland.

PEO-05.old: Stakeholder work is not a one-time list. The uploaded materials emphasize early identification, analysis of power/interest and engagement, tailored communication, and continuous monitoring.
PEO-05.summary: Stakeholders are the people who affect your project or are affected by it. You care because finding them early and involving them in the right way prevents surprises and resistance later.
PEO-05.example: A finance director who was never consulted starts blocking approvals. Wei adds her to the stakeholder register (list of stakeholders), meets her to learn her concerns, and sets up a short monthly review with her.
dos: Identify stakeholders early and keep looking for new ones
Analyze each one's power, interest and expectations
Tailor how you engage each stakeholder
Update the stakeholder register as things change
donts: Do not send more messages without understanding the resistance.
Do not treat the stakeholder register as a one-time list.
Do not escalate a resistant stakeholder before analyzing why.
Do not engage everyone the same way.
PEO-05.examCue: When a question says 'new stakeholder', 'resistant' or 'high power', think: identify, analyze their concern, then engage. Update the register first.

PEO-06.old: Communication notes emphasize tailoring method and frequency to stakeholder needs, active listening, and correcting structural communication problems through the communications approach rather than reactive messaging.
PEO-06.summary: Communication means getting the right information to the right people in a way they can use. You care because most project problems begin with someone not knowing something they needed to know.
PEO-06.example: Executives say Tom's 12-page weekly report tells them nothing. He asks what they need to decide, replaces it with a one-page dashboard, and asks a month later whether it helps.
dos: Ask who needs what information, and why
Tailor method, detail and frequency to each audience
Listen actively: repeat back, clarify, then solve
Update the communications plan when communication keeps failing
donts: Do not assume more communication fixes the problem.
Do not use one channel for every stakeholder.
Do not send a blaming memo instead of fixing the process.
Do not leave a remote team without agreed communication rules.
PEO-06.rule: Audience → Need → Method → Frequency → Feedback → Adjust
PEO-06.examCue: When a question says 'misunderstanding', 'did not receive' or 'virtual team', think: find why it failed, then review the communications management plan.

PEO-07.old: The leadership and roles materials distinguish formal authority from influence. The PM often works through expert and referent power, while decision rights depend on governance and delivery context.
PEO-07.summary: Authority is the formal right to decide; influence is getting things done through trust and knowledge. You care because a PM often has little formal authority and must know who owns each decision.
PEO-07.example: Ravi needs a tester who reports to a department manager. He cannot order her onto his project. He meets the manager, explains the need and timing, and they agree two days a week.
dos: Check who owns the decision before acting
Use your knowledge and relationships to influence
Negotiate with functional managers for people
Escalate only when an authority gap remains
donts: Do not assume the PM owns every decision.
Do not use escalation in place of influence.
Do not use threats or punishment except as a last resort.
Do not tell an agile team who does which task.
PEO-07.rule: Problem → Check role/authority → Engage owner → Act → Escalate if gap remains
PEO-07.examCue: When a question says 'functional manager', 'product owner' or 'no formal authority', think: who owns this decision? Then influence with expert or referent power.

PEO-08.old: Coaching is used to improve capability and performance without taking ownership away from the team. The uploaded materials emphasize feedback, psychological safety, mentoring, and helping teams improve their own process.
PEO-08.summary: Coaching means helping a person or team improve their own performance without taking the work away from them. You care because the exam prefers private, supportive conversations over punishment.
PEO-08.example: Mei has missed three deadlines. Carlos does not raise it in the team meeting. He talks with her privately, learns she never got training on the new tool, arranges it, and checks in each week.
dos: Observe the performance gap first
Talk privately to understand the cause
Clarify expectations and coach or arrange training
Follow up, and escalate formally only if unresolved
donts: Do not criticize a person in front of others.
Do not replace someone before you understand the cause.
Do not take over the team's work yourself.
Do not go to HR or the manager as your first step.
PEO-08.examCue: When a question says 'underperforming', 'missed deadlines' or 'behavior issue', think: private conversation first, find the cause, then coach.

PEO-09.old: The lifecycle notes distinguish Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, Sprint Review, Retrospective, and Daily Scrum. Review concerns the product and stakeholders; retrospective concerns the team's process.
PEO-09.summary: In Scrum, three roles and a few regular meetings keep an agile team moving. You care because exam questions test who decides what and which meeting is for which purpose.
PEO-09.example: A manager asks Lena's team to add a feature mid-sprint. Lena, the Scrum Master, points him to the Product Owner, who owns the priority list. The team keeps working, and the feature is ordered in the backlog.
dos: Send new requests and priorities to the Product Owner
Let the Developers decide how to do the work
Use the Sprint Review for product feedback from stakeholders
Use the Retrospective to improve how the team works
donts: Do not turn the Daily Scrum into a status meeting for managers.
Do not let stakeholders run the Retrospective.
Do not assign daily tasks to a self-managing team.
Do not confuse the Sprint Review with the Retrospective.
PEO-09.rule: Plan → Build → Inspect daily → Review product → Improve process
PEO-09.examCue: When a question says 'feedback on the product' think Sprint Review; 'improve how we work' think Retrospective; 'priority' or 'backlog order' think Product Owner.

PRO-01.old: The foundations and flow materials emphasize integration: the PM connects scope, schedule, cost, quality, resources, risk, stakeholders, procurement, and value instead of optimizing one area in isolation.
PRO-01.summary: Integration means keeping all parts of the project working together: scope, schedule, cost, quality, risk and people. You care because a fix in one area almost always affects another.
PRO-01.example: The client wants delivery two weeks earlier. Before saying yes, Ben checks what that does to cost, testing and risk. He shows the trade-offs, gets the change approved, and updates every affected plan.
dos: Assess the impact across the whole project first
Use data to understand performance before acting
Update all related plans after an approved change
Choose what is best for the overall project
donts: Do not fix the schedule at the expense of quality or value.
Do not change one plan and leave the others out of date.
Do not act on one department's goal alone.
Do not decide before you understand the data.
PRO-01.rule: Data → Analyze → Insight → Decision → Action → Monitor
PRO-01.examCue: When a question says 'impact on other areas', 'trade-off' or 'approved change', think integration: assess the whole project, then update all plans.

PRO-02.old: Scope notes distinguish requirements, acceptance criteria, RTM, scope statement, WBS, WBS dictionary, and formal handling of requested changes.
PRO-02.summary: Scope is all the work the project will do, and requirements are what stakeholders need from it. You care because unapproved extra work, called scope creep, is a top cause of trouble.
PRO-02.example: During a website build, the client asks a developer for an extra chat feature. Zoe first checks whether it is in the approved scope. It is not, so she assesses the impact and submits a change request.
dos: Clarify the request and check it against approved scope
Trace each requirement from need to acceptance
Break the scope into smaller pieces with a WBS
Send new scope through the change process
donts: Do not add work informally because it sounds reasonable.
Do not update the baseline before the change is approved.
Do not confuse the RTM (tracing) with the WBS (breaking down).
Do not deliver extras nobody asked for.
PRO-02.rule: Need → Requirement → Acceptance Criteria → Scope/WBS → Deliver → Verify → Accept
PRO-02.examCue: When a question says 'new feature', 'customer asked the team directly' or 'not in scope', think: assess the impact, then follow change control.

PRO-03.old: Schedule learning should connect activity logic, dependencies, float, critical path, and compression trade-offs rather than treating formulas as isolated facts.
PRO-03.summary: A schedule shows the order of the work and how tasks depend on each other. The critical path, the longest chain of tasks, sets the finish date, so that is where you focus.
PRO-03.example: A bridge project is three weeks late. Aisha finds the delay is on the critical path, in steel delivery. She compares adding a second crew with overlapping two tasks, weighs cost against risk, and picks one.
dos: Find the critical path before acting
Check float (spare time) on each activity
Compare crashing and fast tracking by cost and risk
Use spare float before extending the schedule
donts: Do not speed up work that is not on the critical path.
Do not assume crashing and fast tracking have the same effect.
Do not forget fast tracking adds rework risk.
Do not forget crashing adds cost.
PRO-03.rule: Late → Critical path → Options → Trade-offs → Act
PRO-03.examCue: When a question says 'behind schedule', 'no extra budget' or 'add resources', think critical path first: fast tracking adds risk, crashing adds cost.

PRO-04.old: The EVM material teaches the story first: Plan it → Earn it → Spend it → Forecast it. PV, EV, and AC unlock the formulas, followed by variance/index and EAC/ETC/VAC interpretation.
PRO-04.summary: Earned value management (EVM) compares the work you planned, the work you finished and the money you spent. It tells you early whether you are over budget or behind schedule.
PRO-04.example: By month three, Hana planned $50,000 of work, finished $40,000 worth and spent $45,000. She is behind and over budget. She finds the cause, forecasts the final cost, and reports it to the sponsor.
dos: Find PV, EV and AC first
Start every variance and index formula with EV
Read above 1 as good and below 1 as bad
Forecast the final cost (EAC), then decide how to respond
donts: Do not read schedule variance as days; it is in money.
Do not use a forecast formula without checking its assumption.
Do not confuse the cost baseline with the project budget.
Do not report numbers without saying what they mean.
PRO-04.rule: Plan it → Earn it → Spend it → Forecast it
PRO-04.examCue: When a question gives 'CPI' or 'SPI', think: below 1 is bad, above 1 is good. CPI is cost, SPI is schedule.

PRO-05.old: The quality materials frame quality as conformance + fitness for use, with prevention over inspection. They distinguish Manage Quality, Control Quality, and formal acceptance.
PRO-05.summary: Quality means the product meets its requirements and is fit for use. You care because preventing defects costs less than finding them later, and the customer must formally accept the result.
PRO-05.example: A team finishes a payroll report. Testers check it against requirements and it passes. Yuki then reviews it with the payroll manager, who signs off. Only then does Yuki treat it as accepted.
dos: Build quality into the process from the start
Check the deliverable against requirements (Control Quality)
Get formal acceptance from the customer (Validate Scope)
Find the root cause of defects
donts: Do not assume internal testing equals customer acceptance.
Do not treat quality as a final inspection only.
Do not add extras and call it quality (gold plating).
Do not confuse low grade with low quality.
PRO-05.rule: Plan quality → Build quality → Check quality → Accept quality
PRO-05.examCue: When a question says 'verified' think Control Quality by the team; 'accepted' or 'sign-off' think Validate Scope with the customer; 'process' think Manage Quality.

PRO-06.old: The Risk materials distinguish future uncertainty from current issues and organize work around identification, qualitative/quantitative analysis, responses, reserves, and monitoring.
PRO-06.summary: A risk is something that might happen in the future; an issue is a problem happening now. You care because each one has its own path and its own log.
PRO-06.example: Ivan listed 'supplier may deliver late' as a risk with a backup supplier ready. The supplier does miss the date. Ivan records it in the issue log, activates the backup supplier, and updates the risk register.
dos: Ask first: has it happened yet?
Record and analyze risks in the risk register
Carry out the planned response when a risk occurs
Log it as an issue and keep monitoring
donts: Do not leave a risk that has occurred only in the risk register.
Do not ignore new risks created by your response.
Do not re-analyze a current problem as if it might happen.
Do not treat every risk as a threat.
PRO-06.rule: No → Risk: Analyze → Respond → Monitor. Yes → Issue: Analyze → Resolve → Monitor.
PRO-06.examCue: When a question says 'might', 'could' or 'potential', think risk register. 'Has occurred' or 'is happening' means issue log and act now.

PRO-07.old: Reserve notes distinguish contingency reserve from management reserve and connect funding decisions to identified vs unforeseen uncertainty.
PRO-07.summary: Reserves are extra money or time set aside for uncertainty: contingency reserve for risks you identified, management reserve for surprises nobody saw coming. You need to know which one applies and who approves it.
PRO-07.example: A storm delays a build. Storm delay was in the risk register, so Kofi uses the contingency reserve. Later a surprise soil problem appears. That was never identified, so he asks the sponsor for management reserve.
dos: Ask whether the risk was identified beforehand
Use contingency reserve for identified risks
Request management reserve for unforeseen events
Update the records after using a reserve
donts: Do not use management reserve for every overrun.
Do not spend a reserve without the required approval.
Do not use a reserve to avoid a necessary change request.
Do not place management reserve inside the cost baseline.
PRO-07.rule: Identified risk → Contingency reserve. Unforeseen → Management reserve, with approval.
PRO-07.examCue: When a question says 'identified risk' or 'known', think contingency reserve. 'Unforeseen' or 'unknown' means management reserve, which needs approval.

PRO-08.old: The procurement cheat sheet emphasizes clear scope, right contract, fair selection, active monitoring, formal change, and clean closure.
PRO-08.summary: Procurement is buying goods or services from outside your organization. You care because the contract sets the rules for both sides, so most answers begin with reading the contract.
PRO-08.example: A seller delivers servers two weeks late and blames the buyer. Elena reads the contract first, gathers the facts, and talks with the seller. They agree on a fix and she records the change formally.
dos: Define what you need clearly in the statement of work
Choose the contract type by scope clarity and risk
Select sellers with the agreed criteria
Review the contract before acting on any dispute
donts: Do not choose a seller on lowest price alone.
Do not mix up buyer documents (RFP) with seller responses (proposal).
Do not skip project change control when a contract change affects baselines.
Do not escalate before reviewing the contract.
PRO-08.rule: Clear scope → right contract → fair selection → monitoring → formal change → clean closure
PRO-08.examCue: When a question says 'seller', 'claim' or 'dispute', think contract first. Fixed price puts risk on the seller; cost reimbursable puts it on the buyer.

PRO-09.old: Resource questions often test negotiation, role authority, continuity, knowledge transfer, and the schedule effect of leveling/smoothing.
PRO-09.summary: Resources are the people and equipment your project needs, and most of them are shared with other work. You care because getting, keeping and replacing people without hurting the schedule is your job.
PRO-09.example: Priya, your only database expert, is pulled onto another project by her department manager. You check what her absence does to your dates, then meet that manager to agree on shared hours and a handover to a colleague.
dos: Find out who controls the person: often the functional (department) manager.
Assess the impact on schedule and cost before you talk to anyone.
Negotiate with the resource owner first; escalate only if that fails.
Plan knowledge transfer when someone is leaving or being replaced.
donts: Do not assume the charter lets you overrule a functional manager.
Do not run to the sponsor before you have tried to negotiate.
Do not let a person leave without handing over what they know.
Do not forget: leveling can move the end date; smoothing stays within float (spare time).
PRO-09.rule: Need/Conflict → Assess impact → Negotiate → Adjust/Transfer → Escalate if unresolved
PRO-09.examCue: When a question says 'functional manager', 'resource conflict' or 'overallocated', think: assess the impact, then negotiate with the resource owner before escalating.

PRO-10.old: The document deck provides a compact memory system: WHY = Business Case; AUTHORITY = Charter/Governance; HOW = Management Plan; APPROVED = Baseline; MAY HAPPEN = Risk Register; HAPPENED = Issue Log; TRACE = RTM; DETAIL = WBS Dictionary; CHANGE STATUS = Change Log; SELLER = Contract.
PRO-10.summary: Every project document answers one question: why, who has authority, how, what was approved, what may happen, what did happen. You care because the exam asks which document to open or update.
PRO-10.example: A supplier misses a delivery on Maria's office move. That has already happened, so she records it in the issue log, not the risk register. The new delivery date changes her approved schedule, so she raises a change request.
dos: Ask what the scenario needs: why, authority, how, approved target, or tracking.
Use a management plan for how the work will be managed.
Use a baseline as the approved target you measure against.
Update registers and logs freely as things change.
donts: Do not pick a document because its name sounds close.
Do not edit a baseline freely; it changes only through approved change control.
Do not treat a log entry as an approval.
Do not mix them up: risk register = may happen; issue log = already happened.
PRO-10.rule: WHY = Business Case; AUTHORITY = Charter; HOW = Plan; APPROVED = Baseline; TRACK = Register/Log
PRO-10.examCue: When a question says 'which document', 'update' or 'refer to', think: what question does it answer? Why, authority, how, approved, may happen, or happened.

PRO-11.old: Change control material repeatedly emphasizes sequence: analyze impact before approval or implementation, follow the defined authority path, then update and communicate.
PRO-11.summary: Integrated change control is the agreed path every change must follow before it touches the approved plan. You care because unapproved changes quietly break scope, schedule and budget.
PRO-11.example: The sponsor asks Dev to add a reporting screen next week. Dev thanks him, works out the extra cost and days with the team, submits a change request, and builds it only after the change control board (the approving group) says yes.
dos: Understand the change and analyze its impact before anything else.
Submit a change request to the right approval authority.
Update plans, baselines and the change log after approval.
Tell affected stakeholders what was decided, then implement and monitor.
donts: Do not implement first and analyze later.
Do not go to the change control board without an impact analysis.
Do not skip the process because the sponsor or customer asked.
Do not change a baseline casually or on your own.
PRO-11.rule: Change identified → Impact analysis → Change request → Decision → Update/Communicate → Implement → Monitor
PRO-11.examCue: When a question says 'new request', 'CCB' or 'baseline affected', think: analyze impact first, then follow the formal change process.

PRO-12.old: The lifecycle deck uses a memorable spectrum: Predictive = know it/plan it; Iterative = improve it; Incremental = add to it; Agile = learn/adapt; Hybrid = blend what fits.
PRO-12.summary: These are five ways to run a project, from planning everything up front to learning as you go. You care because picking the wrong approach for the work causes rework, delay and unhappy stakeholders.
PRO-12.example: A bank builds a new branch and a mobile app together. Ana plans the building up front because the design is fixed. Her app team delivers in short cycles because customers keep changing what they want. That blend is hybrid.
dos: Check how stable the requirements are before choosing.
Use predictive when the work is well understood and change is costly.
Use agile when needs are evolving and frequent feedback helps.
Combine approaches on purpose when parts of the work differ.
donts: Do not pick agile because it sounds modern.
Do not treat hybrid as random mixing; each part needs a reason.
Do not assume predictive means no change, or agile means no planning.
Do not confuse iterative (improve the same thing) with incremental (add usable pieces).
PRO-12.rule: Predictive = plan it; Iterative = improve it; Incremental = add to it; Agile = adapt
PRO-12.examCue: When a question says 'stable requirements', think predictive. 'Evolving' or 'frequent feedback', think agile. 'Some parts fixed, some changing', think hybrid.

PRO-13.old: The lifecycle notes distinguish Scrum cadence from Kanban flow. Scrum uses sprints and defined accountabilities/events; Kanban visualizes flow, limits WIP, and measures throughput/cycle time.
PRO-13.summary: Scrum works in fixed time boxes called sprints with set roles and meetings. Kanban is continuous flow with limits on work in progress (WIP). You care because each uses different measures and fixes.
PRO-13.example: A support team's board shows eight tickets stuck in 'Testing' when the limit is five. Sam does not let anyone start new tickets. He asks the team to help clear testing first, then looks for the cause.
dos: Decide first: is this about sprints and roles, or about flow?
Use velocity (work finished per sprint) for Scrum teams.
Use throughput and cycle time (start-to-finish time) for Kanban.
Help finish stuck work when a WIP limit is exceeded.
donts: Do not use velocity as a Kanban measure.
Do not start more work when WIP is already over the limit.
Do not assume every board is Kanban; without WIP limits it is only a task board.
Do not add sprints or sprint events to a pure Kanban question.
PRO-13.rule: Scrum = cadence and sprints; Kanban = flow, WIP limits and pull.
PRO-13.examCue: When a question says 'sprint' or 'velocity', think Scrum. When it says 'WIP', 'bottleneck' or 'cycle time', think Kanban.

az-note-people-02.old: In agile environments, the leader enables the team rather than directing every task.
az-note-people-02.summary: Servant leadership means you lead by helping the team succeed instead of giving orders. You care because PMI treats this as the default style, especially on agile teams.
az-note-people-02.example: Lena's developers are waiting three days for a test server. She does not tell them what to do meanwhile. She calls the infrastructure lead, gets the server released, and keeps a demanding executive from interrupting them.
dos: Remove impediments (things blocking the team).
Coach the team and let them make their own work decisions.
Protect the team from outside interruptions.
Stay active: ask what the team needs and act on it.
donts: Do not assign tasks to each person yourself.
Do not make every team decision for them.
Do not think servant leader means passive; you still act and remove blockers.
Do not solve a problem the team can solve with a little coaching.
az-note-people-02.rule: Serve the team so the team can deliver value.
az-note-people-02.examCue: When a question says 'blocked', 'impediment' or 'self-organizing team', think: remove the obstacle and coach, do not command.

az-note-people-03.old: Know how team behavior changes through forming, storming, norming, performing, and adjourning.
az-note-people-03.summary: Teams grow through five stages: forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. You care because the right leadership move depends on which stage the team is in.
az-note-people-03.example: Three weeks into a project, two analysts argue openly about who owns the test plan. Omar recognizes storming. He brings them together, clarifies roles, and helps them agree on how they will work.
dos: Give clear direction while the team is forming.
Expect conflict in storming and help the team work through it.
Step back and delegate once the team is performing.
Watch for a slide back to storming when membership changes.
donts: Do not treat all conflict as failure; storming is normal.
Do not expect a brand-new team to perform at full speed.
Do not use one style for every stage.
Do not skip closing and recognition when the team adjourns.
az-note-people-03.examCue: When a question says 'new team', 'arguing over roles' or 'new member joined', think: which Tuckman stage, then match your style to it.

az-note-people-04.old: The PM should understand stakeholder needs, influence, expectations, and engagement before choosing a communication response.
az-note-people-04.summary: Stakeholder engagement means working with the people your project affects so they support it. You care because one ignored or unhappy stakeholder can stall the whole project.
az-note-people-04.example: A warehouse supervisor keeps criticizing a new scanning system in meetings. Grace does not send another status email. She meets him, learns he fears losing staff, and involves him in planning the training.
dos: Identify stakeholders and analyze their interest and influence.
Tailor how you engage each person to what they need.
Meet resistant stakeholders to understand their real concern.
Reassess engagement as the project and the people change.
donts: Do not use the same communication approach for everyone.
Do not ignore or work around a resistant stakeholder.
Do not treat stakeholder analysis as a one-time task.
Do not confuse sending information with engaging people.
az-note-people-04.rule: Analyze first; engage intentionally; monitor continuously.
az-note-people-04.examCue: When a question says 'resistant', 'unaware' or 'new stakeholder', think: analyze their needs first, then adjust the engagement approach.

az-note-people-05.old: Choose interactive, push, or pull communication based on urgency, complexity, audience, and need for feedback.
az-note-people-05.summary: There are three ways to share information: interactive (two-way, live), push (you send it) and pull (people fetch it). You care because the wrong method causes misunderstanding and conflict.
az-note-people-05.example: Two team leads are upset about a schedule cut. Ravi does not email them. He holds a call so they can ask questions. The weekly report goes out by email, and the procedures manual sits on the team site.
dos: Use interactive when you need immediate feedback or the topic is sensitive.
Use push, such as email or memos, for routine updates to specific people.
Use pull, such as a shared site, for large reference material.
Check that the message was understood, not only sent.
donts: Do not use email alone for conflict or bad news.
Do not pick the fastest method without asking if it will work.
Do not assume a pushed message was read or understood.
Do not use pull for anything urgent.
az-note-people-05.rule: Complex or sensitive = interactive; broad reference material = pull.
az-note-people-05.examCue: When a question says 'sensitive', 'misunderstanding' or 'urgent', think interactive. 'Large audience' or 'reference library', think pull.

az-note-people-06.old: PMP scenarios often reward self-awareness, empathy, and adapting your approach before reacting.
az-note-people-06.summary: Emotional intelligence is noticing and managing your own feelings and reading other people's. You care because most project problems are people problems, and a calm, understanding response works better.
az-note-people-06.example: In a review, a senior engineer snaps that the plan is unrealistic. Mei does not defend the plan in front of everyone. She pauses, talks to him privately afterwards, and learns he is overloaded on another project.
dos: Pause and notice your own reaction before you speak.
Listen fully before you respond.
Look for the feeling behind the words.
Adapt your message to the person and the moment.
donts: Do not react defensively or take criticism personally.
Do not assume resistance is only about technical facts.
Do not confront someone's emotions in front of the group.
Do not jump to a solution before you understand the person.
az-note-people-06.examCue: When a question says 'frustrated', 'upset' or 'withdrawn', think: listen and understand privately first, then respond.

az-note-people-07.old: Choose the people-development technique based on whether the need is performance, long-term growth, or skill acquisition.
az-note-people-07.summary: These are three ways to help someone grow. Training teaches a missing skill, coaching improves how they perform now, and mentoring guides long-term career growth. Choosing the right one fixes the real gap.
az-note-people-07.example: Jon keeps making errors in a new estimating tool he has never been taught. Sara arranges training on the tool. Later, when he knows the tool but struggles to run client meetings, she coaches him after each one.
dos: Train when a specific skill or knowledge gap exists.
Coach to improve current performance on real work.
Mentor for longer-term career and professional growth.
Find the real gap before you choose.
donts: Do not use training when the issue is motivation or conflict.
Do not mentor when the person needs a skill this week.
Do not replace a struggling person before trying to develop them.
Do not confuse coaching with telling someone exactly what to do.
az-note-people-07.rule: Coach = performance; Mentor = growth; Train = skill.
az-note-people-07.examCue: When a question says 'lacks the skill', think train. 'Not performing well', think coach. 'Career' or 'long-term growth', think mentor.

az-note-people-08.old: Understand what is blocking performance before offering rewards, discipline, or structural changes.
az-note-people-08.summary: Motivation is what makes people want to do good work. You care because rewards or discipline fail when you have not found out what is really holding someone back.
az-note-people-08.example: A reliable tester starts missing deadlines. Carlos does not offer a bonus or a warning. He asks privately what changed, learns she is bored with repeat work, and gives her ownership of the new automation task.
dos: Find the root cause of low performance first.
Talk to the person privately and listen.
Use recognition, growth and autonomy (freedom to decide), not only money.
Create psychological safety, so people can speak up without fear.
donts: Do not assume money is the only motivator.
Do not punish before you understand the cause.
Do not offer the same reward to everyone; people want different things.
Do not report the person to their manager as your first step.
az-note-people-08.rule: Diagnose first; motivate based on the real need.
az-note-people-08.examCue: When a question says 'performance dropped', 'low morale' or 'disengaged', think: find the cause privately before any reward or discipline.

az-note-people-09.old: Remote teams need deliberate communication, trust-building, working agreements, and inclusive collaboration.
az-note-people-09.summary: A virtual team works from different places, often in different time zones and cultures. You care because trust and clear communication do not happen by accident when people never meet.
az-note-people-09.example: Aisha's team is spread across Virginia, Poland and India. She agrees shared core hours with them, rotates meeting times so no one always joins at midnight, and holds a video call when two members disagree.
dos: Agree communication norms and response times with the team.
Choose collaboration tools on purpose and make sure everyone can use them.
Plan around time zones and cultural differences.
Build trust with regular live contact.
donts: Do not assume silence means agreement.
Do not handle conflict only through email or chat.
Do not schedule every meeting for one location's convenience.
Do not leave remote members out of decisions and recognition.
az-note-people-09.rule: Make expectations visible when the team is not co-located.
az-note-people-09.examCue: When a question says 'remote', 'time zones' or 'distributed team', think: clear norms, the right tools, and live conversation for sensitive issues.

az-note-people-10.old: PMP negotiation questions favor preparation, interests over positions, and mutually beneficial outcomes.
az-note-people-10.summary: Negotiation is reaching an agreement both sides can live with. You care because you negotiate daily for people, dates, scope and contracts, and the relationship continues afterwards.
az-note-people-10.example: A vendor demands two extra weeks. Nina asks why and learns their installer is booked. She offers to receive the equipment early so their second crew can install it. Both sides keep their dates.
dos: Prepare: know your limits and what you can trade.
Ask why the other side wants what they want.
Look for options where both sides win.
Use objective criteria, such as contract terms or data.
donts: Do not begin with threats or escalation.
Do not focus only on stated positions; find the interest behind them.
Do not win in a way that damages the relationship.
Do not give up something you have no authority to give.
az-note-people-10.rule: Interests first, options next, agreement last.
az-note-people-10.examCue: When a question says 'disagree on terms', 'vendor' or 'functional manager', think: understand interests, then look for a win-win option.

az-note-people-11.old: Use an appropriate decision method and involve the right people based on urgency and expertise.
az-note-people-11.summary: Decision making is choosing how a choice gets made and who makes it. You care because involving the wrong people, or too many, slows the project and weakens commitment.
az-note-people-11.example: The team must choose between two testing tools. Ben does not pick one himself. He confirms the team has authority to choose, lets them vote after a short discussion, and records the decision and the reasons.
dos: Clarify who has the authority to decide.
Involve the team when their commitment matters.
Match the method to urgency and expertise.
Record important decisions and the reasons.
donts: Do not seek consensus for every minor decision.
Do not bypass governance (the approval rules) for convenience.
Do not decide alone on matters the team must own.
Do not make a decision that belongs to the sponsor or change board.
az-note-people-11.rule: Right people + right authority + right method.
az-note-people-11.examCue: When a question says 'team cannot agree', 'who should decide' or 'urgent decision', think: authority first, then the method that fits.

az-note-people-12.old: Teams perform better when expectations for behavior, communication, and collaboration are explicit.
az-note-people-12.summary: Ground rules, or working agreements, are the team's own rules for behaving and working together. You care because clear shared expectations prevent friction and give you something to point to when it appears.
az-note-people-12.example: Half the team keeps arriving late to the daily meeting. Tara does not announce a new rule. She raises it with the team, they agree to start on time and keep cameras on, and add it to their team charter.
dos: Create the rules together with the team, early.
Write them in the team charter where everyone can see them.
Refer back to them when behavior slips.
Revisit and update them when problems appear.
donts: Do not impose rules without team input, unless company policy requires it.
Do not write them once and never look again.
Do not be the only one who enforces them; the whole team shares that.
Do not confuse them with the project charter, which authorizes the project.
az-note-people-12.rule: Agree early on how the team will work together.
az-note-people-12.examCue: When a question says 'repeated behavior problem', 'late to meetings' or 'new team', think: team charter and ground rules, set by the team.

az-note-people-13.old: Adapt leadership style to the team, context, urgency, and delivery approach.
az-note-people-13.summary: A leadership style is how you guide people, from giving close direction to stepping back. You care because the same style that helps a new team will frustrate an experienced one.
az-note-people-13.example: Kofi's new interns need step-by-step guidance on the test scripts, so he directs them closely. His senior developers know the work well, so he agrees the goal with them and gets out of their way.
dos: Match your style to the team's experience and maturity.
Give more direction to new or struggling team members.
Facilitate and delegate with experienced teams.
Shift your style as the team develops.
donts: Do not use one leadership style for every situation.
Do not micromanage a mature, self-organizing team.
Do not leave a new team without direction.
Do not choose a command style on the exam unless there is a real emergency.
az-note-people-13.examCue: When a question says 'new team member', 'experienced team' or 'crisis', think: match the style to maturity and urgency. Default to servant leadership.

az-note-people-14.old: PMP increasingly rewards giving teams authority within clear boundaries.
az-note-people-14.summary: Empowerment means giving the team real authority to decide how they do their work, within clear limits. You care because trusted teams decide faster and own their results.
az-note-people-14.example: The team chooses a different test approach than Hana would have picked. It fits the budget and the quality standard, so she lets it stand. She asks them to show results at the next review.
dos: Make the decision limits clear: budget, quality, deadlines.
Let the team own how the work is done.
Support them and hold them accountable for results.
Give them the information they need to decide well.
donts: Do not take back a decision because you would do it differently.
Do not empower without setting boundaries.
Do not confuse empowering with abandoning; stay available.
Do not blame the team for a mistake made within the limits you set.
az-note-people-14.examCue: When a question says 'team decided', 'self-organizing' or 'PM disagrees with the approach', think: respect the team's decision if it is within the agreed limits.

az-note-people-15.old: When resources are constrained, understand priorities and negotiate rather than escalating immediately.
az-note-people-15.summary: A resource conflict happens when two pieces of work need the same person or equipment at once. You care because how you resolve it affects your schedule and your working relationships.
az-note-people-15.example: Two projects both need the only network engineer in the same week. Luis checks which tasks can wait without moving his end date, then meets the engineer's department manager to agree which days each project gets.
dos: Review priorities and what each side really needs.
Check the resource management plan for how conflicts are handled.
Negotiate with the functional (department) manager.
Replan the work, then escalate only if it stays unresolved.
donts: Do not bypass the functional manager and go to the person directly.
Do not secretly overload the team with overtime.
Do not escalate to the sponsor as your first move.
Do not ignore the schedule impact of the fix you agree.
az-note-people-15.rule: Assess → Negotiate → Replan → Escalate if unresolved.
az-note-people-15.examCue: When a question says 'shared resource', 'pulled to another project' or 'functional manager refuses', think: assess, then negotiate before escalating.

az-note-process-01.old: Know exactly who owns value, process facilitation, and delivery work in Scrum.
az-note-process-01.summary: Scrum has three roles: the Product Owner decides what is built and in what order, the Scrum Master looks after the process, and the Developers decide how. Many exam answers hinge on who owns what.
az-note-process-01.example: A sales director asks a developer to slip in an extra feature this sprint. The Scrum Master steps in and sends the director to the Product Owner, who decides where the request sits in the product backlog.
dos: Send requests about what to build to the Product Owner.
Let the Scrum Master coach the team and remove impediments (blockers).
Let the Developers decide how to do the work.
Respect each role's boundary when you are the project manager.
donts: Do not let the Scrum Master prioritize the backlog.
Do not have a project manager assign tasks to individual developers.
Do not let the Product Owner dictate how the work is performed.
Do not let stakeholders go around the Product Owner.
az-note-process-01.rule: PO = What/Priority · Scrum Master = Process · Developers = How.
az-note-process-01.examCue: When a question says 'priority' or 'new request', think Product Owner. 'Impediment', think Scrum Master. 'How to build', think Developers.

az-note-process-02.old: Understand the purpose of Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Sprint Retrospective.
az-note-process-02.summary: Scrum has four regular meetings inside each sprint: Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. Each has one purpose, and the exam tests whether you take a problem to the right one.
az-note-process-02.example: After a sprint, customers say the new search screen is confusing, and the team says handoffs were messy. The screen feedback is discussed in the Sprint Review. The handoff problem goes to the Retrospective.
dos: Use Sprint Planning to select work and set a Sprint Goal.
Use the Daily Scrum for the Developers to plan the next day.
Use the Review to show the increment (finished work) to stakeholders.
Use the Retrospective to improve how the team works.
donts: Do not confuse the Review (product) with the Retrospective (process).
Do not turn the Daily Scrum into a status report for a manager.
Do not skip the Retrospective when the sprint went well.
Do not solve problems inside the Daily Scrum; take them outside the meeting.
az-note-process-02.examCue: When a question says 'stakeholder feedback' or 'demo', think Sprint Review. 'Process problem' or 'how we work', think Retrospective.

az-note-process-03.old: The Product Backlog is ordered by value; the Sprint Backlog is owned and adapted by Developers during the sprint.
az-note-process-03.summary: The Product Backlog is the ordered list of everything the product might need. The Sprint Backlog is the team's plan for the current sprint. Knowing who owns each tells you where new requests go.
az-note-process-03.example: Mid-sprint, a manager asks the team to add a report right away. The Developers do not add it. The request goes to the Product Owner, who places it in the Product Backlog for a future sprint.
dos: Let the Product Owner order the Product Backlog by value.
Let the Developers own and adjust the Sprint Backlog.
Refine backlog items continuously so they are ready.
Route new requests to the Product Owner.
donts: Do not freeze the Product Backlog; it changes throughout the project.
Do not let stakeholders insert work directly into the sprint.
Do not let the Product Owner change the Sprint Backlog; Developers own it.
Do not raise a formal change request for a backlog change on an agile team.
az-note-process-03.rule: Product Backlog = evolving priorities; Sprint Backlog = current sprint plan.
az-note-process-03.examCue: When a question says 'new requirement', 'mid-sprint request' or 'reprioritize', think: Product Owner adds it to the Product Backlog.

az-note-process-04.old: Acceptance criteria describe a specific item; Definition of Done is the shared quality standard for completed work.
az-note-process-04.summary: Acceptance criteria are the conditions one specific item must meet. The Definition of Done (DoD) is the shared quality checklist every item must pass. Work is finished only when both are met.
az-note-process-04.example: A login story meets its acceptance criteria: users can sign in with email. But it has not been code-reviewed, which the team's Definition of Done requires. So the team does not call it done or show it at the review.
dos: Check both acceptance criteria and the DoD before calling work complete.
Agree acceptance criteria with the Product Owner for each item.
Keep the DoD visible and the same for every item.
Return unfinished items to the Product Backlog.
donts: Do not treat acceptance criteria and the DoD as the same thing.
Do not count work as done when it meets only one of them.
Do not relax the DoD to finish a sprint on time.
Do not show partly done work as finished at the Sprint Review.
az-note-process-04.rule: Acceptance criteria = item-specific; DoD = team-wide quality bar.
az-note-process-04.examCue: When a question says 'is it done', 'almost complete' or 'passed testing but', think: both acceptance criteria and Definition of Done must be met.

az-note-process-05.old: Kanban optimizes flow by visualizing work, limiting work in progress, and managing bottlenecks.
az-note-process-05.summary: Kanban is a way to manage work by showing it on a board and limiting work in progress (WIP), the items started but not finished. Finishing work, not starting it, delivers value.
az-note-process-05.example: The 'Review' column on a marketing team's board is full, and writers want to start new articles. Joy asks two writers to help review the waiting drafts first. Then the team looks at why review is slow.
dos: Visualize the workflow on a board everyone can see.
Respect the WIP limit for each column.
Clear bottlenecks (stuck points) before starting more work.
Pull new work only when there is capacity.
donts: Do not keep everyone busy by starting everything at once.
Do not ignore a blocked or overfull column.
Do not raise the WIP limit to hide a bottleneck.
Do not push work onto people; in Kanban the team pulls it.
az-note-process-05.examCue: When a question says 'WIP exceeded', 'bottleneck' or 'work piling up', think: stop starting, help finish, then find the cause.

az-note-process-06.old: A cumulative flow diagram shows work distribution over time and helps reveal bottlenecks and WIP growth.
az-note-process-06.summary: A cumulative flow diagram (CFD) is a chart of colored bands showing how many items sit in each work stage over time. It shows where work is piling up.
az-note-process-06.example: On the team's chart, the 'In Test' band has grown wider for three weeks while 'Done' stays flat. Raj sees that testing is the bottleneck. He raises it with the team, and they move one developer to help test.
dos: Look for a widening band as the bottleneck signal.
Check that the 'Done' band keeps rising steadily.
Use the chart with the team to discuss how stable the flow is.
Find the cause before you change anything.
donts: Do not read it like a burndown chart; its lines go up, not down.
Do not blame the people in the widening stage; look at the flow.
Do not start more work when a band is widening.
Do not use it to track cost or budget.
az-note-process-06.rule: Widening band = work accumulating in that state.
az-note-process-06.examCue: When a question says 'band is widening', 'flow over time' or 'where is work piling up', think cumulative flow diagram and a bottleneck.

az-note-process-07.old: Burndown shows work remaining; burnup shows work completed against total scope and makes scope change easier to see.
az-note-process-07.summary: Both charts track agile progress. A burndown shows how much work is left; a burnup shows work finished against the total scope line. The burnup lets you see when scope was added.
az-note-process-07.example: Maria's team finishes 20 points each sprint, yet the burndown barely drops. She opens the burnup chart and sees the total scope line jumped twice. The team is fine, new stories were added, and she shows this to the product owner.
dos: Use a burndown to see how much work is left.
Use a burnup when scope keeps growing or shrinking.
Check the scope line before judging the team's pace.
Share the chart openly so everyone sees progress.
donts: Do not blame the team for a flat burndown before checking for added scope.
Do not read a burnup as work remaining; it shows work completed.
Do not hide the chart when the trend looks bad.
az-note-process-07.rule: Burndown = work left. Burnup = work done + total scope line.
az-note-process-07.examCue: When a question says "scope was added" or "progress looks stalled", think burnup chart, because it shows the scope line separately.

az-note-process-08.old: Velocity is a team-specific planning aid based on completed story points; it is not a productivity score.
az-note-process-08.summary: Velocity is how many story points (size units for work) one team finishes in a sprint, on average. The team uses it to forecast how much it can take on next.
az-note-process-08.example: Dev's team finished 28, 32 and 30 points in the last three sprints. The product owner asks how long 150 points will take. Dev uses the average of 30 and answers: about five sprints.
dos: Use the team's own past sprints to forecast.
Compare a team only with its own history.
Let velocity settle over a few sprints before trusting it.
Find the blocker when velocity drops.
donts: Do not compare velocity between two teams; their points are sized differently.
Do not use velocity to rate individual people.
Do not set a higher velocity as a target; teams inflate points.
Do not count unfinished stories in velocity.
az-note-process-08.rule: Velocity forecasts; it does not rank teams or people.
az-note-process-08.examCue: When a question says "how many sprints" or "compare team velocity", think forecasting for one team only, never a productivity score.

az-note-process-09.old: Relative estimation focuses on size, complexity, and uncertainty rather than false precision.
az-note-process-09.summary: Agile teams estimate by comparing items to each other, using story points (size units for work), instead of guessing exact hours. The whole team estimates together, so the numbers reflect shared understanding.
az-note-process-09.example: Priya's team plays planning poker on a login story. Two people show 3 and one shows 13, so Priya asks the high and low voters to explain. They learn about a hidden security step and agree on 8.
dos: Let the people doing the work give the estimate.
Compare each item to one the team already finished.
Discuss big differences in estimates before agreeing.
Update estimates as the team learns more.
donts: Do not let the manager or product owner set the estimates.
Do not turn story points into hours or individual performance scores.
Do not average the votes to skip the discussion.
Do not treat an early estimate as a promise.
az-note-process-09.rule: The team estimates together, by relative size, and refines as it learns.
az-note-process-09.examCue: When a question says "story points", "planning poker" or "estimates differ widely", think team discussion and relative size, not exact hours.

az-note-process-10.old: Hybrid combines predictive and agile approaches based on the nature of the work rather than ideology.
az-note-process-10.summary: Hybrid means using a plan-driven approach for the parts that are well known and an agile approach for the parts that are still unclear. The PM picks the mix on purpose, part by part.
az-note-process-10.example: A hospital is adding a new wing with a patient app. Carlos plans the building work up front with fixed approvals. The app team works in two-week sprints with nurse feedback, and both report to one steering group.
dos: Identify which parts need control and which need flexibility.
Choose the approach for each part based on its uncertainty.
Keep one set of approvals and reporting across both.
Explain the mix to stakeholders early.
donts: Do not force all the work into one life cycle.
Do not mix methods at random; hybrid is a deliberate choice.
Do not assume agile is always better or predictive always safer.
Do not skip required approvals on the agile part.
az-note-process-10.rule: Hybrid = control where required, adapt where beneficial.
az-note-process-10.examCue: When a question says "fixed regulatory requirements" plus "unclear features", think hybrid: predictive for the known part, agile for the uncertain part.

az-note-process-11.old: A risk is uncertain and may occur; an issue has already occurred and needs action now.
az-note-process-11.summary: A risk is something that might happen in the future. An issue is a problem that has already happened and needs action now. The PM tracks them in different places and handles them differently.
az-note-process-11.example: Ana listed "supplier may ship late" in the risk register with a backup supplier. On Monday the supplier confirms a two-week delay, so it is now an issue. Ana records it in the issue log, assigns an owner, and starts the backup plan.
dos: Record future uncertainty in the risk register.
Record a confirmed problem in the issue log.
Carry out the planned response when a risk happens.
Assign an owner and a due date to every issue.
donts: Do not leave a risk that already happened only in the risk register.
Do not start risk analysis on a problem that is already here; act.
Do not assume every issue needs a change request.
Do not wait for the next meeting to log an issue.
az-note-process-11.rule: Risk register = future uncertainty. Issue log = current problems.
az-note-process-11.examCue: When a question says "might", "could" or "possible", think risk. When it says "has occurred" or "is now", think issue log.

az-note-process-12.old: Match the response strategy to whether the risk is a threat or opportunity and assign ownership.
az-note-process-12.summary: A risk response is what you plan to do about a risk before it happens. Threats and opportunities each have five choices, and every risk needs one named owner.
az-note-process-12.example: Lena's project depends on one crane. She buys insurance for crane damage (transfer), schedules extra maintenance (mitigate), and names the site lead as risk owner. He watches for warning signs each week.
dos: Pick a response for each important risk.
Assign one owner to each risk.
Plan a fallback in case the first response fails.
Escalate risks that are outside the project's authority.
donts: Do not mix up mitigate (lower the chance or impact) with avoid (remove the threat).
Do not think transfer removes the risk; it moves who pays.
Do not use exploit for a threat; exploit and enhance are for opportunities.
Do not leave a risk without an owner.
az-note-process-12.rule: Choose a response → assign an owner → watch the trigger.
az-note-process-12.examCue: When a question says "insurance" or "outsource", think transfer. "Reduce probability" means mitigate. "Change the plan to remove it" means avoid.

az-note-process-13.old: Contingency reserve covers identified risks; management reserve covers unknown-unknowns and is outside the cost baseline.
az-note-process-13.summary: Both are extra money set aside for uncertainty. Contingency reserve covers risks you already identified and sits inside the cost baseline. Management reserve covers total surprises and needs approval from above the PM.
az-note-process-13.example: Tom budgeted $10,000 contingency for bad weather, but storms cost $15,000. He spends the contingency and submits a change request for the extra $5,000. He does not dip into the management reserve, because weather was a known risk.
dos: Use contingency reserve for identified risks.
Ask for approval before using management reserve.
Submit a change request when a known risk costs more than its contingency.
Review remaining reserves as risks pass.
donts: Do not treat management reserve as normal project money.
Do not use management reserve for a risk you had identified.
Do not count management reserve inside the cost baseline.
Do not spend contingency on extra features.
az-note-process-13.rule: Contingency = known risks. Management reserve = unknown risks.
az-note-process-13.examCue: When a question says "identified risk", think contingency. When it says "unforeseen" or "not anticipated", think management reserve and approval.

az-note-process-14.old: In predictive work, assess impact before approval and update baselines only after authorized change approval.
az-note-process-14.summary: Change control is the step-by-step way a predictive project handles a requested change. The PM studies the impact first, gets approval from the right authority, and only then updates the plan.
az-note-process-14.example: A sponsor asks Rita to add a new report. Rita writes a change request, works with the team to find the cost and schedule impact, and sends it to the change control board (the approving group). After approval she updates the plan and tells the team.
dos: Write the change request down.
Analyze impact on scope, schedule, cost, quality and risk with the team.
Send it to the approving authority named in the plan.
Update the baselines and inform stakeholders after approval.
donts: Do not start the work before the change is approved.
Do not reject a change before assessing its impact.
Do not update baselines without approval, even for the sponsor.
Do not go to the board before analyzing with the team.
az-note-process-14.examCue: When a question says "sponsor requests", "customer wants to add" or "small change", think analyze the impact first, then the change control board.

az-note-process-15.old: Resolve issues at the lowest appropriate level, but escalate when authority, urgency, or impact exceeds the team’s limits.
az-note-process-15.summary: Escalating means taking a problem to someone with more authority. The PM first tries to understand and solve it at the team level, and escalates only when it is beyond their power.
az-note-process-15.example: A vendor refuses to deliver unless the contract price changes. Sam checks the contract, talks to the vendor, and confirms he cannot approve more money. He takes the facts and two options to the sponsor and records the decision.
dos: Assess the problem and its impact first.
Check whether you have the authority to solve it.
Use the escalation path defined for the project.
Bring facts and options when you escalate.
donts: Do not escalate to the sponsor as the first step.
Do not hide a problem that is beyond your authority.
Do not skip levels or go around the agreed path.
Do not decide something that belongs to someone else.
az-note-process-15.rule: Problem → Assess → Check → Owner → Act → Escalate.
az-note-process-15.examCue: When a question says "what should the PM do first", think assess and talk. When it says "outside the PM's authority", think escalate.

az-note-process-16.old: Requirements define needs; the scope baseline controls approved project scope in predictive projects.
az-note-process-16.summary: Requirements are what stakeholders need. The scope baseline is the approved description of the work: the scope statement, the WBS (work broken into pieces) and its dictionary. The PM builds exactly that, nothing extra.
az-note-process-16.example: A developer wants to add a free dashboard the customer never asked for. Mei says no and explains it is not in the approved scope. When the customer later asks for it, Mei submits a change request.
dos: Trace each requirement back to a business need.
Compare the work against the approved scope baseline.
Send every scope change through change control.
Confirm finished deliverables with the customer.
donts: Do not gold plate (add unrequested extras), even to please the customer.
Do not add a small request informally; that is scope creep.
Do not change the baseline without approval.
Do not collect requirements from only one stakeholder.
az-note-process-16.rule: Build only approved scope: no gold plating, no scope creep.
az-note-process-16.examCue: When a question says "team added an extra feature", think gold plating. When it says "customer asked informally", think change request.

az-note-process-17.old: Control Quality checks correctness; Validate Scope obtains formal acceptance.
az-note-process-17.summary: Control Quality is the team checking that the deliverable is built correctly. Validate Scope is the customer or sponsor formally accepting it. The team's check comes first.
az-note-process-17.example: Omar's team finishes a training manual. A team member checks it against the quality checklist and fixes two errors. Then Omar walks the customer through it, and the customer signs the acceptance form.
dos: Check the deliverable against requirements before showing the customer.
Fix defects found during the internal check.
Get formal sign-off from the customer or sponsor.
Keep the signed acceptance as a record.
donts: Do not ask for acceptance before the quality check is done.
Do not treat a passed inspection as customer acceptance.
Do not leave Validate Scope until project closing; do it per deliverable.
Do not confuse Control Quality with Manage Quality, which looks at the process.
az-note-process-17.rule: Control Quality = correct. Validate Scope = accepted. Quality first, acceptance second.
az-note-process-17.examCue: When a question says "formal acceptance" or "customer sign-off", think Validate Scope. "Inspection" or "meets requirements" means Control Quality.

az-note-process-18.old: The critical path determines the shortest project duration; activities on it generally have zero total float.
az-note-process-18.summary: The critical path is the longest chain of linked activities, and it sets the earliest date the project can finish. Float is how long an activity can slip without delaying the finish.
az-note-process-18.example: Nina's project has two paths: one of 20 days and one of 14. A task on the 14-day path runs three days late. Nina checks and sees it had six days of float, so the finish date holds, and she keeps watching the 20-day path.
dos: Find the longest path through the schedule first.
Check an activity's float before reacting to a delay.
Focus any time-saving effort on critical path activities.
Recheck the path after every schedule change.
donts: Do not call the critical path the shortest path; it is the longest.
Do not shorten an activity with float and expect an earlier finish.
Do not forget that using up float can create a new critical path.
Do not ignore near-critical paths.
az-note-process-18.rule: Critical path = longest path, zero float. Float = flexibility.
az-note-process-18.examCue: When a question says "zero float" or "will the delay affect the end date", think critical path and check the float first.

az-note-process-19.old: Fast tracking overlaps sequential work and increases risk; crashing adds resources/cost to shorten duration.
az-note-process-19.summary: Both are ways to shorten a schedule without cutting scope. Fast tracking does steps in parallel that were planned one after another. Crashing adds people or money to finish sooner.
az-note-process-19.example: Leo must finish three weeks early. He starts painting upstairs while wiring is still going on downstairs (fast tracking). When that is not enough and the sponsor approves more budget, he adds a second crew (crashing).
dos: Check which activities are on the critical path first.
Weigh the extra cost or risk before choosing.
Try fast tracking first when no extra budget exists.
Crash the activity with the lowest cost per day saved.
donts: Do not call adding resources fast tracking; that is crashing.
Do not compress an activity that is not on the critical path.
Do not forget fast tracking raises the risk of rework.
Do not crash without approval for the extra cost.
az-note-process-19.rule: Fast track = overlap, more risk. Crash = more resources, more cost.
az-note-process-19.examCue: When a question says "additional budget is available", think crashing. When it says "no extra money" or "in parallel", think fast tracking.

az-note-process-20.old: Know the direction of CPI and SPI and what EV, PV, and AC represent.
