az-note-process-20.summary: Earned value compares three numbers: work you planned (PV), work you finished (EV), and money you spent (AC). From them the PM sees whether the project is over budget or behind schedule.
az-note-process-20.example: Halfway through, Kim has finished $40,000 of work, planned $50,000, and spent $45,000. CPI = 40/45 = 0.89 and SPI = 40/50 = 0.80. She is over budget and behind, so she looks for the cause.
dos: Calculate CPI as EV divided by AC.
Calculate SPI as EV divided by PV.
Read a value above 1 as good news.
Find the cause before choosing a corrective action.
donts: Do not flip the formula; EV always goes on top.
Do not read a CPI below 1 as under budget.
Do not mix up AC (money spent) with PV (work planned).
Do not report the numbers without explaining the cause.
az-note-process-20.rule: CPI < 1 = over budget. SPI < 1 = behind schedule. EV comes first.
az-note-process-20.examCue: When a question gives EV, AC and PV, think CPI for money and SPI for schedule; below 1 is bad, above 1 is good.

az-note-process-21.old: Prevent defects through quality planning and process improvement rather than relying only on inspection.
az-note-process-21.summary: Quality management means planning how to meet requirements and building the work the right way the first time. Preventing a defect costs less than finding and fixing it later.
az-note-process-21.example: Testers keep finding the same data-entry errors each month. Instead of adding more testers, Zoe gives the team a checklist and a short training. The errors drop, and less rework is needed.
dos: Build quality checks into the daily work.
Look for the cause when a defect repeats.
Improve the process, not only the product.
Agree on quality standards with stakeholders up front.
donts: Do not rely only on inspection at the end.
Do not add extra features and call it quality; that is gold plating.
Do not confuse Manage Quality (process) with Control Quality (deliverable).
Do not skip inspection entirely; it still matters.
az-note-process-21.rule: Prevention over inspection. Manage Quality = process; Control Quality = product.
az-note-process-21.examCue: When a question says "defects keep recurring" or "rework is rising", think prevention and fixing the process, not more inspection.

az-note-process-22.old: Fix the underlying cause, not merely the visible symptom.
az-note-process-22.summary: Root cause analysis means finding the real reason a problem happened, not only what you can see. Fix the real reason and the problem stops coming back.
az-note-process-22.example: A website crashes every Friday, and the team restarts it each time. Ravi asks "why?" five times and learns a weekly backup fills the disk. He moves the backup to another disk, and the crashes stop.
dos: Gather the facts before suggesting a fix.
Ask "why" repeatedly until you reach the real cause.
Use a fishbone diagram to sort possible causes.
Check later that the fix worked.
donts: Do not jump to a solution before confirming the cause.
Do not treat the symptom and call it solved.
Do not blame a person when the process caused it.
Do not skip checking that the fix held.
az-note-process-22.rule: Symptom ≠ root cause. Find the cause, then fix.
az-note-process-22.examCue: When a question says "recurring problem" or "keeps happening", think root cause analysis: 5 Whys or a fishbone diagram.

az-note-process-23.old: Understand where cost risk sits in fixed-price, cost-reimbursable, and time-and-materials contracts.
az-note-process-23.summary: The contract type decides who pays if the work costs more than expected. In fixed price the seller carries that risk; in cost-reimbursable the buyer does; time and materials sits in between.
az-note-process-23.example: Ben needs a warehouse roof replaced, and the drawings are complete. He picks a fixed-price contract, so the roofer absorbs any overrun. For early research with unclear scope, he would pay actual costs plus a fee instead.
dos: Choose fixed price when the scope is clear.
Choose cost-reimbursable when the scope is still uncertain.
Use time and materials for small or urgent work with a cap.
Track the seller's work against the contract terms.
donts: Do not change contract work informally; use the contract change process.
Do not pick fixed price when the scope is unclear.
Do not think cost-reimbursable protects the buyer; the buyer carries the cost risk.
Do not leave a time and materials contract without a not-to-exceed limit.
az-note-process-23.rule: Fixed price = seller's risk. Cost-reimbursable = buyer's risk. T&M = shared.
az-note-process-23.examCue: When a question says "well-defined scope", think fixed price. "Scope unclear" means cost-reimbursable. "Staff needed quickly" means time and materials.

az-note-process-24.old: Consider capability, cost, schedule, risk, strategic value, and organizational constraints before sourcing.
az-note-process-24.summary: Make-or-buy is deciding whether your own team does the work or you pay an outside seller. The PM compares cost, skills, time, risk and long-term value, not price alone.
az-note-process-24.example: Sara needs a payroll module, and her team could build it in six months, but they have never done payroll rules. A vendor offers a proven product in six weeks. Sara compares total cost and risk, and recommends buying.
dos: Compare the full cost of making versus buying.
Check whether the team has the skills and time.
Consider risk, schedule and long-term support.
Record the reasons for the decision.
donts: Do not choose on the lowest starting price alone.
Do not ignore support and maintenance costs after delivery.
Do not buy when the work is core knowledge the organization must keep.
Do not skip the organization's procurement rules.
az-note-process-24.rule: Best choice = value + risk + capability, not price alone.
az-note-process-24.examCue: When a question says "team lacks the skill" or "lowest bid", think make-or-buy analysis: total cost, risk and capability.

az-note-process-25.old: Clarify who performs, approves, contributes, and is informed to reduce ownership confusion.
az-note-process-25.summary: A RACI chart lists each task and who is Responsible (does it), Accountable (owns the result), Consulted (gives input) and Informed (kept updated). It ends confusion over who does what.
az-note-process-25.example: Two team leads each think the other is approving the test plan, so nobody does. Aisha builds a RACI chart with the team. One lead is named Accountable, the other Consulted, and the plan is approved that week.
dos: Name exactly one Accountable person for each task.
Build the chart together with the team.
Use it to settle overlaps in who owns what.
Update it when roles or people change.
donts: Do not give one task two Accountable people.
Do not mix up Responsible (does the work) with Accountable (answers for it).
Do not treat a RACI chart as a tool for fixing stakeholder engagement.
Do not leave a task with nobody Responsible.
az-note-process-25.examCue: When a question says "unclear roles", "duplicate work" or "nobody owns it", think RACI chart with one Accountable person.

az-note-process-26.old: Retrospectives improve the team’s way of working and should produce actionable experiments.
az-note-process-26.summary: A retrospective is a short team meeting at the end of each sprint to look at how the team worked. The team picks one or two changes to try next sprint.
az-note-process-26.example: Stories keep getting stuck waiting for review, so in the retrospective Hana asks what slowed the team down. They agree to review each other's work within one day. Next sprint, Hana checks whether it helped.
dos: Make it safe for people to speak honestly.
Pick one or two improvements to try.
Give each improvement an owner.
Check at the next retrospective whether it worked.
donts: Do not turn the meeting into a blame session.
Do not confuse it with the sprint review, which looks at the product.
Do not wait until project end to improve the process.
Do not let the manager dictate the improvements.
az-note-process-26.rule: Inspect the process, adapt the process. Review = product; retrospective = process.
az-note-process-26.examCue: When a question says "agile team process problem" or "how the team works", think retrospective. "Demo to stakeholders" means sprint review.

az-note-process-27.old: Refinement improves clarity and readiness; prioritization should reflect value, risk, dependencies, and stakeholder needs.
az-note-process-27.summary: The backlog is the ordered list of work still to do. Refinement makes items clear and small enough to start; prioritization puts the most valuable items at the top. The product owner decides the order.
az-note-process-27.example: A story called "improve checkout" is too big to estimate. In refinement, the team and product owner Elena split it into three small stories with clear acceptance tests. Elena moves the payment fix to the top because customers are leaving.
dos: Split large items into small, clear ones.
Add acceptance criteria (how we know it is done).
Help the product owner order items by value and risk.
Reorder as new information arrives.
donts: Do not treat the backlog order as fixed.
Do not let the team or PM set priority; the product owner does.
Do not pull an unclear item into a sprint.
Do not add new work to a sprint in progress; put it in the backlog.
az-note-process-27.rule: Refine continuously; the product owner orders by value and risk.
az-note-process-27.examCue: When a question says "new request during a sprint" or "story too large", think backlog: product owner prioritizes, team refines.

az-note-business-03.old: The business case explains why the project should exist and whether continued investment remains justified.
az-note-business-03.summary: The business case explains why the project is worth doing: the need, the options, the costs, the benefits and the risks. The PM keeps checking that the reason still holds.
az-note-business-03.example: Jo's project builds a store kiosk to cut checkout time. Midway, the company moves to mobile-only checkout. Jo reviews the business case with the sponsor, since the expected benefit may be gone, and the sponsor decides what happens next.
dos: Read the business case to learn why the project exists.
Recheck it after any major change.
Raise it with the sponsor when the benefit looks doubtful.
Tie project decisions back to the expected benefits.
donts: Do not treat the business case as a one-time kickoff document.
Do not confuse it with the charter, which authorizes the project.
Do not cancel or continue the project on your own; the sponsor decides.
Do not judge value by money alone; compliance and safety count.
az-note-business-03.rule: Business case = why. Charter = authorizes. If the why disappears, reassess.
az-note-business-03.examCue: When a question says "justification", "why the project exists" or "benefits no longer expected", think business case and talk to the sponsor.

az-note-business-06.old: Projects should remain aligned to organizational strategy and intended outcomes.
az-note-business-06.summary: Strategic alignment means the project still supports what the organization is trying to achieve. A project that finishes on time but no longer serves that goal is not a success.
az-note-business-06.example: Paul is building a tool for a product line. The company announces it will sell that line. Paul does not push on; he assesses what the news means for the project and takes it to the sponsor for a decision.
dos: Link each project objective to an organizational goal.
Assess the impact when the strategy changes.
Tell the sponsor when the project may no longer fit.
Keep the team informed of why the work matters.
donts: Do not keep going just because the plan was approved.
Do not make a major strategic decision alone.
Do not measure success by on time and on budget only.
Do not escalate before you have assessed the impact.
az-note-business-06.rule: A successful project must still be the right project.
az-note-business-06.examCue: When a question says "strategy changed" or "new company priorities", think assess the impact, then reassess the project with the sponsor.

az-note-business-07.old: Market, regulatory, economic, social, and technology changes can alter project assumptions and value.
az-note-business-07.summary: Things outside the project keep changing: laws, markets, the economy, technology, competitors. Any of them can change what the project needs to deliver, so the PM watches and reacts.
az-note-business-07.example: A new privacy law is announced while Ines's team builds a customer app. Ines checks how it affects the requirements, adds the new risks to the risk register, and raises a change request for the extra consent screens.
dos: Watch for outside changes that touch the project.
Assess the impact on scope, risk and benefits.
Treat compliance changes as mandatory.
Raise a change request when the plan must change.
donts: Do not assume the approved plan is safe from outside change.
Do not ignore a new regulation because it costs time.
Do not change the plan without assessing the impact first.
Do not wait for the sponsor to notice the change.
az-note-business-07.rule: Scan the environment → assess the impact → update the plan.
az-note-business-07.examCue: When a question says "new regulation", "market shift" or "competitor", think assess the impact on the project first, then follow change control.

az-note-business-08.old: Project closure should prepare the receiving organization to sustain the delivered capability.
az-note-business-08.summary: Transition means handing the finished product to the people who will run it every day. The project is not really done until they can use and support it.
az-note-business-08.example: Before the new booking system goes live, Maya trains the front-desk staff, gives the support team a user guide, and agrees who answers questions after launch. The operations manager signs the handover, and then Maya closes the project.
dos: Plan training, documentation and support before go-live.
Get the receiving team's sign-off.
Agree who owns the benefits after the project ends.
Capture lessons learned before releasing the team.
donts: Do not close the project just because the deliverables are built.
Do not treat handoff as the end of value; benefits come later.
Do not release the team before the handover is accepted.
Do not assume people will use it without training.
az-note-business-08.rule: No adoption, no benefits. Finish by enabling operations.
az-note-business-08.examCue: When a question says "users are not using it" or "who owns benefits after closure", think transition: training, handover and a benefits owner.

TW-001.old: Helps people understand, adopt, and sustain a new way of working. Think resistance, communication, training, engagement, readiness, and reinforcement.
TW-001.hook: Is it about people adopting, or about changing the approved plan?
TW-001.leftMeaning: Helping people understand, accept and keep using a new way of working. Think training, communication and handling resistance.
TW-001.rightMeaning: The formal steps to review, approve or reject a change to the approved plan: scope, schedule or cost.
TW-001.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the new payroll system works fine, but clerks keep using their old spreadsheets and say nobody trained them.
TW-001.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the sponsor asks for an extra report that will add two weeks and more cost to the approved schedule.
TW-001.rightMemory: Change Control = plan changes get approved.
TW-001.trap: Staff resisting a new system is not fixed by a change request. And strong user support is not permission to alter a baseline without approval.
TW-001.memory: CHANGE MANAGEMENT = people adopt. CHANGE CONTROL = project changes are governed.

TW-002.old: Focuses on how people adopt a new capability, process, system, or behavior.
TW-002.hook: Are people struggling to adopt, or is the plan itself changing?
TW-002.leftMeaning: A change in how people work: a new system, process or habit that staff must take up.
TW-002.rightMeaning: A change to the project or product itself that affects requirements, scope, schedule, cost or risk.
TW-002.leftScenarioCue: You see this when nurses avoid the new scheduling tool after go-live and managers ask how to win them over.
TW-002.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the client wants a new feature added, and the PM must check its effect on cost and dates.
TW-002.trap: A rollout with unhappy employees is not automatically a baseline problem. Look for resistance first; raise a change request only if the plan must change.
TW-002.memory: People resist → organizational change. Baseline affected → project change/control.

TW-003.old: An uncertain future event or condition that may affect objectives.
TW-003.hook: Might it happen, or has it already happened?
TW-003.leftMeaning: Something uncertain in the future that could help or hurt the project if it occurs.
TW-003.rightMeaning: A problem that is happening now or has already happened and needs an owner and action.
TW-003.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the supplier warns that a strike next month could delay the steel delivery.
TW-003.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the steel delivery did not arrive this morning and the crew is standing idle.
TW-003.rightMemory: Rain through the roof = Issue Log.
TW-003.trap: Once the event has happened, stop treating it as a future risk. Log it as an issue, assign an owner and act.
TW-003.memory: MAY HAPPEN = Risk Register. HAPPENED = Issue Log.

TW-004.old: Describes HOW an area of the project will be planned, managed, monitored, or controlled.
TW-004.hook: Does it describe how we work, or the approved target?
TW-004.leftMeaning: A document that says HOW one area, such as scope, cost or risk, will be planned, managed and controlled.
TW-004.rightMeaning: The approved version of scope, schedule or cost that actual results are measured against.
TW-004.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a new team member asks how change requests are submitted and who approves them.
TW-004.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the PM compares actual spending with the approved budget to see how far off the project is.
TW-004.leftMemory: Plan = how we will do it.
TW-004.trap: They are not the same thing. Adjusting how you manage is different from changing an approved target, which needs formal change control.

TW-005.old: A formal proposal to modify a document, deliverable, baseline, process, or other controlled element.
TW-005.hook: Is it asking for a change, or tracking what happened?
TW-005.leftMeaning: A formal request to change something controlled, such as a deliverable, a document or a baseline.
TW-005.rightMeaning: The running list of every change request and its status: pending, approved, rejected or deferred.
TW-005.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a team lead fills in a form asking to swap a material and explains the cost impact.
TW-005.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a stakeholder asks whether last month's requested change was approved or rejected.
TW-005.trap: Writing a request in the log does not approve it. Rejected requests are recorded there too, so check the status before doing the work.
TW-005.memory: REQUEST asks for change. LOG tracks what happened to the request.

TW-006.old: Has been checked for correctness and conformance to requirements through quality control.
TW-006.hook: Did we check it, or did the customer approve it?
TW-006.leftMeaning: A finished deliverable the team has inspected and found correct against the requirements.
TW-006.rightMeaning: A deliverable the customer or sponsor has formally signed off as meeting the acceptance criteria.
TW-006.leftScenarioCue: You see this when testers finish inspecting the training manual and confirm it meets every requirement.
TW-006.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the customer walks through the finished manual and signs the acceptance form.
TW-006.trap: Passing the team's own quality check is not customer acceptance. The deliverable is verified first, then taken to the customer for sign-off.
TW-006.memory: VERIFY = we checked it. ACCEPT = they approved it.

TW-007.old: Checks deliverables for correctness, completeness, and conformance to quality requirements.
TW-007.hook: Is the team checking correctness, or the customer formally accepting?
TW-007.leftMeaning: The team's own check that a deliverable is correct and meets its quality requirements.
TW-007.rightMeaning: The step where the customer or sponsor formally accepts the completed deliverable.
TW-007.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team inspects a batch of circuit boards and measures them against the defect limits.
TW-007.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the PM meets the customer to review a finished deliverable and get written sign-off.
TW-007.trap: Quality always happens before validation. Do not ask the customer to accept a deliverable the team has not yet checked.
TW-007.memory: QUALITY checks it. SCOPE accepts it.

TW-008.old: Explains why the initiative is worth doing and supports the investment decision.
TW-008.hook: Is it why we invest, or how we prove the value?
TW-008.leftMeaning: The document that explains why the project is worth the money: need, options, costs, benefits and risks.
TW-008.rightMeaning: The plan for which benefits are expected, how and when they are measured, and who owns them.
TW-008.leftScenarioCue: You see this when leaders ask whether the project is still worth funding after costs rise sharply.
TW-008.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the system is live and someone must measure whether call times actually dropped after six months.
TW-008.rightMemory: Benefits = what value, when, who owns.
TW-008.trap: Finishing the deliverable does not prove the benefits arrived. Benefits are measured, often after the project closes, by a named owner.
TW-008.memory: BUSINESS CASE = why. BENEFITS = what value, when, how measured, who owns it.

TW-009.old: Defines decision rights, authority, oversight, escalation paths, and who can approve what.
TW-009.hook: Is it who may decide, or a rule that must be followed?
TW-009.leftMeaning: The framework of authority: who can approve, who oversees, and where to escalate.
TW-009.rightMeaning: Meeting the laws, regulations, standards and policies the project is required to follow.
TW-009.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the PM is unsure whether the sponsor or the steering committee may approve a budget increase.
TW-009.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a safety regulation requires an inspection that would delay the launch by a week.
TW-009.trap: A senior person's approval does not remove a legal requirement. Value or urgency never justifies skipping approvals or mandatory rules.
TW-009.memory: GOVERNANCE = WHO DECIDES. COMPLIANCE = WHAT MUST BE FOLLOWED.

TW-010.old: Refines the same solution through repeated versions or cycles.
TW-010.hook: Are we improving the same thing, or adding new pieces?
TW-010.leftMeaning: Building the same solution again in repeated cycles, improving it each time using feedback.
TW-010.rightMeaning: Delivering the solution in usable pieces, adding a new working part each time.
TW-010.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a design team shows three versions of the same screen, each better after user feedback.
TW-010.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a banking app releases login first, then payments, then statements, each usable on its own.
TW-010.trap: Prototypes that keep getting better are iterative. New usable features arriving one after another are incremental. Agile does both together.

TW-011.old: Uses frequent feedback, adaptation, small increments, collaboration, and evolving requirements.
TW-011.hook: Is the whole project adaptive, or a deliberate mix?
TW-011.leftMeaning: An adaptive way of working: short cycles, frequent customer feedback and requirements that can change.
TW-011.rightMeaning: A deliberate mix of predictive (plan up front) and adaptive methods, chosen to fit each part of the work.
TW-011.leftScenarioCue: You see this when requirements are unclear and the customer wants to review working software every two weeks.
TW-011.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a hospital builds its new wing with a fixed plan but develops the patient app in sprints.
TW-011.trap: Hybrid is not random mixing, and Agile is not working without a plan. Match the approach to how certain the work is.
TW-011.memory: AGILE = learn and adapt. HYBRID = blend what fits.

TW-012.old: Inspects the product/increment and discusses progress and next product directions with stakeholders.
TW-012.hook: Are we inspecting the product, or how the team works?
TW-012.leftMeaning: The team shows the finished work to stakeholders and gathers feedback on the product.
TW-012.rightMeaning: The team meets privately to discuss how it worked and picks improvements for the next sprint.
TW-012.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team demonstrates the new checkout feature and the customer suggests what to build next.
TW-012.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the team discusses why handoffs kept slipping and agrees to try a new working rule.
TW-012.trap: Customer feedback on the product belongs in the Review. A problem with how the team works belongs in the Retrospective.

TW-013.old: Ordered, evolving list of product work and needs.
TW-013.hook: Is it everything the product may need, or this sprint's work?
TW-013.leftMeaning: The ordered, always-changing list of everything the product may need. The Product Owner owns it.
TW-013.rightMeaning: The work the Developers selected for this sprint, with the Sprint Goal and their plan to deliver it.
TW-013.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a stakeholder asks for a new feature and the Product Owner must decide where it ranks.
TW-013.rightScenarioCue: You see this when developers at the daily standup look at the tasks they committed to finishing this sprint.
TW-013.rightMemory: Sprint Backlog = what we do now.
TW-013.trap: A new request goes to the Product Owner and the Product Backlog, not straight into the sprint. The Sprint Backlog can adjust, but the Sprint Goal stays.
TW-013.memory: PRODUCT BACKLOG = what may come. SPRINT BACKLOG = the team's work now.

TW-014.old: Identifies stakeholders and records relevant characteristics such as interest, influence, or impact.
TW-014.hook: Is it who they are, or how we will involve them?
TW-014.leftMeaning: The list of who the stakeholders are, with their interest, influence and impact on the project.
TW-014.rightMeaning: The plan for how to involve each stakeholder and move them toward the support the project needs.
TW-014.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a new department head joins and the PM records her role, interest and influence.
TW-014.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a key manager is resistant and the PM decides how to bring him to support the project.
TW-014.rightMemory: Engagement Plan = how we involve them.
TW-014.trap: Listing a stakeholder is not the same as planning how to win their support. A new stakeholder goes in the register first; then update the plan.

TW-015.old: Requirements Traceability Matrix links requirements from origin through delivery, verification, and acceptance.
TW-015.hook: Are we tracing a requirement, or breaking down the work?
TW-015.leftMeaning: The Requirements Traceability Matrix: a table linking each requirement to its source, deliverable, test and acceptance.
TW-015.rightMeaning: The Work Breakdown Structure: a tree that breaks the whole project scope into small deliverable pieces called work packages.
TW-015.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a requirement changes and the PM checks which deliverables and test cases are connected to it.
TW-015.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the team splits a new website into design, content and hosting pieces to estimate each one.
TW-015.trap: The RTM does not track tasks, and the WBS does not trace requirements. Ask whether you are following one requirement or dividing the work.
TW-015.memory: RTM = TRACE requirements. WBS = BREAK DOWN scope.

TW-016.hook: Do you need the picture, or the details behind a box?
TW-016.leftMeaning: The tree diagram that breaks the project scope into deliverables and work packages.
TW-016.rightMeaning: The companion document that describes each WBS item: the work, owner, acceptance criteria, estimates and assumptions.
TW-016.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the sponsor asks for a one-page view of all the deliverables in the project.
TW-016.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a team member asks what exactly is included in the Site Preparation work package.
TW-016.rightMemory: WBS Dictionary = detail behind each box.
TW-016.trap: The WBS shows names only. When a question asks what a work package includes or who owns it, look in the WBS Dictionary.

TW-017.old: Request for Information: used to learn about supplier capabilities, offerings, or the market before defining a procurement approach.
TW-017.hook: Are you still learning the market, or asking for a solution?
TW-017.leftMeaning: Request for Information: asks sellers what they can offer, so the buyer can learn the market before buying.
TW-017.rightMeaning: Request for Proposal: asks sellers to propose how they would solve the need, with approach and price.
TW-017.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the buyer does not yet know which vendors can provide drone inspection services at all.
TW-017.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the buyer knows the need and wants vendors to explain how they would build the system.
TW-017.leftMemory: RFI = tell me what is possible.
TW-017.rightMemory: RFP = propose how you would solve it.
TW-017.trap: An RFI gathers information only and does not select a seller. Do not send an RFP when you are still exploring the market.
TW-017.memory: RFI = tell me what is possible. RFP = propose how you'd solve it.

TW-018.old: Used when the buyer needs sellers to propose an approach or solution.
TW-018.hook: Do you need their approach, or only their price?
TW-018.leftMeaning: Request for Proposal: used when the solution is not fixed and sellers must propose their approach.
TW-018.rightMeaning: Request for Quotation: used when the specifications are clear and standard, and price is the main comparison.
TW-018.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the buyer wants vendors to design a custom training program and explain their method.
TW-018.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the buyer needs 200 identical laptops with a set specification and wants the best price.
TW-018.trap: Clear, standard specifications with a focus on price point to an RFQ. A complex need where the approach matters points to an RFP.

TW-019.old: The product, service, result, or deliverable produced.
TW-019.hook: Is it what we delivered, or what changed because of it?
TW-019.leftMeaning: The thing the project produces: a product, service, result or deliverable.
TW-019.rightMeaning: The change that happens when people actually use what was delivered.
TW-019.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team finishes and hands over a new CRM system that works as specified.
TW-019.rightScenarioCue: You see this when sales reps using the new CRM complete their customer follow-ups faster.
TW-019.rightMemory: Outcome = the result of using it.
TW-019.trap: A system can be delivered on time and still change nothing. Low adoption means the outcome was missed, however clean the delivery.
TW-019.memory: Deliverable = what you produce. Outcome = the result of using it.

TW-020.old: The result of using the deliverable, such as customers shifting to self-service.
TW-020.hook: Is it a change in behavior, or a measured gain?
TW-020.leftMeaning: The result of people using the deliverable, such as customers switching to self-service.
TW-020.rightMeaning: The measurable gain that the outcome creates, such as lower support cost or faster service.
TW-020.leftScenarioCue: You see this when most customers start resetting their own passwords instead of calling the help desk.
TW-020.rightScenarioCue: You see this when help desk costs fall by a measured amount because fewer customers call.
TW-020.trap: An outcome is a change you can see; a benefit is a gain you can measure. Neither one is the deliverable itself.

TW-021.old: Budget held for identified risks and known-unknowns that have been analyzed and planned for.
TW-021.hook: Was the risk identified, or was it a total surprise?
TW-021.leftMeaning: Money set aside for risks you already identified and planned for. It sits inside the cost baseline.
TW-021.rightMeaning: Money held outside the cost baseline for surprises nobody identified. Using it usually needs management approval.
TW-021.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a supplier delay listed in the risk register happens and the PM pays for the planned response.
TW-021.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a flood nobody anticipated damages the site and extra funds are needed.
TW-021.trap: If a known risk costs more than its contingency, raise a change request. Do not break open management reserve; it is for unknown risks only.
TW-021.memory: CONTINGENCY = identified risk. MANAGEMENT RESERVE = unforeseen uncertainty.

TW-022.old: Ranks or prioritizes individual risks using relative assessments such as probability, impact, urgency, or other characteristics.
TW-022.hook: Are we ranking risks, or calculating numbers?
TW-022.leftMeaning: Ranks each risk by how likely it is and how much it would affect the project, using high, medium, low.
TW-022.rightMeaning: Uses numbers to estimate the combined effect of risks on cost or schedule, such as expected monetary value.
TW-022.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team rates each risk on a probability and impact grid to pick the top ten.
TW-022.rightScenarioCue: You see this when an analyst runs a simulation to find the chance of finishing within budget.
TW-022.trap: A probability and impact matrix is qualitative, even though it may use scores. Simulations, decision trees and expected monetary value are quantitative.

TW-023.old: A risk that could negatively affect objectives.
TW-023.hook: Would it hurt the project, or help it?
TW-023.leftMeaning: An uncertain event that would harm the project if it happens: a negative risk.
TW-023.rightMeaning: An uncertain event that would help the project if it happens: a positive risk.
TW-023.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a key engineer may leave before testing, which would delay the release.
TW-023.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a new tool might let the team finish a month early if it works.
TW-023.trap: Not every risk should be avoided. Opportunities are exploited, enhanced or shared; threats are avoided, transferred or mitigated. Both can be escalated or accepted.

TW-024.old: Works toward a solution that addresses the underlying concerns of all parties and seeks a durable win-win outcome.
TW-024.hook: Does everyone get what they need, or does each side give something up?
TW-024.leftMeaning: Both sides work on the real problem together until they find an answer that fully works for everyone. A win-win.
TW-024.rightMeaning: Each side gives up part of what it wants so they can meet in the middle. Nobody is fully satisfied.
TW-024.leftScenarioCue: You see this when two leads sit down, share their real concerns, and design a new test plan that meets both the deadline and the quality goal.
TW-024.rightScenarioCue: You see this when two leads both want one tester full time, and they agree to split her week half and half.
TW-024.trap: Compromise sounds fair, so it tempts you. PMI's best answer is usually collaborate, because compromise leaves needs partly unmet. Pick compromise only when time is short.
TW-024.memory: COLLABORATE = solve fully. COMPROMISE = split the difference.

TW-025.old: Influence earned because others trust a person's expertise, experience, or technical knowledge.
TW-025.hook: Do people follow because of what you know, or who you are?
TW-025.leftMeaning: People listen to you because they trust your knowledge, skill and experience.
TW-025.rightMeaning: People listen to you because they respect, like or admire you as a person.
TW-025.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team accepts the PM's network design advice because she ran three similar data center moves before.
TW-025.rightScenarioCue: You see this when team members volunteer to stay late for a PM they admire and trust, though she has no authority over them.
TW-025.trap: Both are earned, not handed out with a job title. Look for the reason people follow: skill and knowledge is expert; respect and admiration is referent.
TW-025.memory: EXPERT = what you know. REFERENT = how people regard you.

TW-026.old: Focuses on serving the team, removing impediments, coaching, facilitating, and enabling self-management.
TW-026.hook: Can the team solve this, or must someone tell them now?
TW-026.leftMeaning: The leader serves the team: removes blockers, coaches, and lets the team organize its own work.
TW-026.rightMeaning: The leader gives clear instructions and watches closely. Useful in an emergency, a safety issue, or with a brand-new team.
TW-026.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a team is stuck waiting on a security approval, and the PM goes to the security office to clear it.
TW-026.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a gas leak is found on site and the PM tells everyone exactly where to go, right now.
TW-026.rightMemory: Directive = tell, when urgent or unsafe.
TW-026.trap: Do not pick command-and-control when the team can solve it together. Servant leadership is PMI's default, and it is active, never passive.

TW-027.old: The buyer/project team creates solicitation and selection artifacts such as procurement SOW, source-selection criteria, RFI, RFQ, RFP, or IFB.
TW-027.hook: Who wrote the document: the one asking, or the one answering?
TW-027.leftMeaning: Documents the buyer writes to ask the market: the work description, the selection criteria, and requests such as RFI, RFQ and RFP.
TW-027.rightMeaning: Documents the seller sends back in answer: information, a price quote, a proposal or a bid.
TW-027.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the PM's team writes an RFP (request for proposal) asking vendors how they would build the payroll system.
TW-027.rightScenarioCue: You see this when three vendors each send in a proposal describing their approach and price for the payroll system.
TW-027.trap: An RFP and a proposal are not the same thing. The buyer issues the request; the seller submits the proposal. Check who is holding the pen.

TW-028.old: Price is largely fixed for defined work; cost overrun risk generally falls more heavily on the seller.
TW-028.hook: Who pays if the work costs more than expected?
TW-028.leftMeaning: One agreed price for clearly defined work. If the work costs more, the seller absorbs the extra.
TW-028.rightMeaning: The buyer pays the seller's real allowed costs plus a fee. If the work costs more, the buyer pays more.
TW-028.leftScenarioCue: You see this when scope is fully defined and a builder agrees to deliver the warehouse for one set price.
TW-028.rightScenarioCue: You see this when research scope is still unclear, so the buyer agrees to pay the lab's actual costs plus a fee.
TW-028.leftMemory: Fixed price = seller carries cost risk.
TW-028.rightMemory: Cost reimbursable = buyer carries cost risk.
TW-028.trap: Do not choose by habit. Clear, stable scope fits fixed price. Unclear or changing scope fits cost reimbursable. Then ask who carries the cost risk.
TW-028.memory: FIXED PRICE = seller bears more cost risk. COST REIMBURSABLE = buyer bears more.

TW-029.old: Evaluates whether work should be performed internally or procured externally.
TW-029.hook: Are we deciding whether to outsource, or which seller to hire?
TW-029.leftMeaning: Deciding if the team should do the work itself or pay an outside company to do it.
TW-029.rightMeaning: Scoring the sellers who responded against agreed criteria to pick the winner.
TW-029.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the PM compares the cost and skills of building the mobile app in-house versus hiring an outside firm.
TW-029.rightScenarioCue: You see this when four proposals have arrived and the panel scores each one on price, experience and technical approach.
TW-029.trap: Order matters. Decide make or buy first, during planning. Compare vendors only after you have chosen to buy and received their responses.
TW-029.memory: MAKE/BUY = internal or external? SOURCE SELECTION = which seller?

TW-030.old: Measures return relative to cost, commonly expressed as a percentage.
TW-030.hook: Is the answer a percentage return, or a dollar value today?
TW-030.leftMeaning: Return on investment: how much you gain compared with what you spent, shown as a percentage.
TW-030.rightMeaning: Net present value: what all future money in and out is worth in today's dollars. Above zero is good.
TW-030.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a sponsor says the project costs $100K, will gain $25K, and asks for the return as a percentage.
TW-030.rightScenarioCue: You see this when two projects pay back over five years and the committee compares what each is worth in today's dollars.
TW-030.trap: They answer different questions. ROI is a rate; NPV is money, adjusted for time. When choosing between projects by NPV, pick the higher positive one.
TW-030.memory: ROI = Return. NPV = Value in dollars today.

TW-031.old: The value of the best alternative you give up when choosing another option.
TW-031.hook: Is it what we gave up, or money already gone?
TW-031.leftMeaning: The value of the best option you did not choose.
TW-031.rightMeaning: Money already spent that you cannot get back. It should not decide what you do next.
TW-031.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the company picks Project A over Project B, and B would have earned $400K. That $400K is what was given up.
TW-031.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a sponsor says, 'We already spent $2 million, so we must finish,' although the product no longer has buyers.
TW-031.trap: Do not keep a weak project alive to justify past spending. Ignore sunk cost and judge future value. Opportunity cost is the whole value of the option not chosen.
TW-031.memory: Opportunity cost = lost alternative. Sunk cost = gone money.

TW-032.old: Capital expenditure for acquiring, creating, or improving long-lived assets or capabilities.
TW-032.hook: Are we buying or building something lasting, or paying to run it?
TW-032.leftMeaning: Capital expenditure: money spent once to buy, build or improve something that lasts for years.
TW-032.rightMeaning: Operating expenditure: the ongoing money needed to run, support and maintain things day to day.
TW-032.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the project buys new servers and builds a data center the company will use for ten years.
TW-032.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the company pays a monthly cloud subscription, support staff and electricity to keep the system running.
TW-032.trap: A cheap purchase can cost a lot to run for years. Look at the full lifetime cost, not only the buying price.

TW-033.old: Focuses on translating the quality plan into executable quality activities and improving processes during execution.
TW-033.hook: Are we improving how we work, or checking what we made?
TW-033.leftMeaning: Turning the quality plan into action during the work: following good processes, auditing them and improving them.
TW-033.rightMeaning: Measuring and testing the finished output to see if it meets the quality requirements.
TW-033.leftScenarioCue: You see this when an audit shows testers skip a required step, and the PM works with the team to fix the process.
TW-033.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a tester measures finished circuit boards against the specification and records which ones pass or fail.
TW-033.leftMemory: Manage Quality = improve how we work.
TW-033.rightMemory: Control Quality = check what we produced.
TW-033.trap: Words like audit, process and improvement point to Manage Quality. Words like inspect, measure and test a deliverable point to Control Quality.
TW-033.memory: MANAGE QUALITY = improve how we work. CONTROL QUALITY = check what we produced.

TW-034.old: Designs work and processes so defects are less likely to occur in the first place.
TW-034.hook: Are we stopping defects before they happen, or finding them after?
TW-034.leftMeaning: Setting up the work so mistakes are less likely to happen in the first place.
TW-034.rightMeaning: Looking at the output to catch mistakes that have already been made.
TW-034.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team is trained and given a checklist before coding starts, so fewer errors are made.
TW-034.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a reviewer examines each finished unit at the end of the line and pulls out the faulty ones.
TW-034.trap: Inspection is necessary, but prevention is preferred. If an answer builds quality in early, it usually beats one that catches defects late.
TW-034.memory: Inspection is necessary. Prevention is preferred.

TW-035.old: Degree to which requirements are fulfilled and the result is fit for its intended use.
TW-035.hook: Does it meet its requirements, or how many features does it have?
TW-035.leftMeaning: How well the result meets its requirements and works for its intended use.
TW-035.rightMeaning: A category for products with the same use but different features or technical level, like basic versus premium.
TW-035.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a basic phone has few features but works perfectly and meets every stated requirement. That is high quality.
TW-035.rightScenarioCue: You see this when a customer chooses between an economy model and a premium model with more features.
TW-035.trap: More features does not mean better quality. A premium product full of defects is high grade but low quality, and low quality is a problem.
TW-035.memory: Low grade can be acceptable. Low quality is not acceptable.

TW-036.old: Planned Value: budgeted value of work that should have been completed by a point in time.
TW-036.hook: Is it work we planned to finish, or work we did finish?
TW-036.leftMeaning: Planned Value: the budgeted worth of the work that should be done by today.
TW-036.rightMeaning: Earned Value: the budgeted worth of the work that is really done by today.
TW-036.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the plan says four of ten rooms, budgeted at $10K each, should be painted by Friday. That is $40K.
TW-036.rightScenarioCue: You see this when only three of those rooms are painted by Friday. The team has earned $30K of budgeted work.
TW-036.rightMemory: EV = what is done, at budget.
TW-036.trap: Neither one is money spent. PV is the plan and EV is completed work valued at budget. Money really spent is AC, actual cost.
TW-036.memory: PV = what should be done. EV = what was completed, valued at budget.

TW-037.old: Earned Value represents the budgeted value of completed work.
TW-037.hook: Is it the budgeted worth of finished work, or money really spent?
TW-037.leftMeaning: Earned Value: the budgeted worth of the work that is finished.
TW-037.rightMeaning: Actual Cost: the real money spent to do that work.
TW-037.leftScenarioCue: You see this when three rooms budgeted at $10K each are painted, so the team has earned $30K of work.
TW-037.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the invoices and timesheets for painting those three rooms add up to $36K paid out.
TW-037.trap: EV is not cash paid. Compare the two: if EV is less than AC, you spent more than the work was worth, so you are over budget.
TW-037.memory: EV = earned work value. AC = actual money spent.

TW-038.old: Cost Performance Index = EV ÷ AC. Below 1 indicates cost inefficiency/over budget relative to earned value.
TW-038.hook: Is the question about money efficiency or schedule efficiency?
TW-038.leftMeaning: Cost Performance Index = EV ÷ AC. It shows how much work you get for each dollar spent. Below 1 means over budget.
TW-038.rightMeaning: Schedule Performance Index = EV ÷ PV. It shows how fast work gets done against the plan. Below 1 means behind schedule.
TW-038.leftScenarioCue: You see this when earned value is $80K and actual cost is $100K. CPI is 0.80, so each dollar buys 80 cents of work.
TW-038.rightScenarioCue: You see this when earned value is $80K and planned value is $100K. SPI is 0.80, so the team is behind plan.
TW-038.trap: Both start with EV on top. Divide by AC for cost and by PV for schedule. Above 1 is good; below 1 is bad.
TW-038.memory: CPI tells money efficiency. SPI tells schedule efficiency.

TW-039.old: Estimate at Completion forecasts total expected project cost when all work is finished.
TW-039.hook: Is it the total cost at the end, or only what is left?
TW-039.leftMeaning: Estimate at Completion: the forecast of the total cost when all the work is finished.
TW-039.rightMeaning: Estimate to Complete: the forecast of the money still needed from today to the finish.
TW-039.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the sponsor asks, 'What will this whole project cost us in the end?' and the PM answers $1.2 million.
TW-039.rightScenarioCue: You see this when $700K is already spent and the sponsor asks, 'How much more money do you need to finish?'
TW-039.rightMemory: ETC = what is left to spend.
TW-039.trap: Do not report the remaining cost as the total. EAC = AC + ETC, so the total always includes money already spent.
TW-039.memory: EAC = Forecast. ETC = Left. EAC = AC + ETC.

TW-040.old: A temporary effort with a defined beginning/end that creates a unique product, service, result, or change.
TW-040.hook: Does the work have an end, or does it repeat every day?
TW-040.leftMeaning: Temporary work with a start and an end that creates something new or unique.
TW-040.rightMeaning: Ongoing, repeating work that keeps the business running day to day.
TW-040.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a hospital builds and launches a new patient portal, then closes the effort once it is live.
TW-040.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the help desk answers patient portal questions every day after it has gone live.
TW-040.trap: Temporary does not mean short. A five-year effort is still a project if it has a defined end and a unique result.
TW-040.memory: PROJECT = change. OPERATIONS = run the business.

TW-041.old: A temporary initiative focused on a specific outcome or deliverable.
TW-041.hook: Is it one effort, or related efforts managed together for shared benefits?
TW-041.leftMeaning: One temporary effort that delivers a specific product, service or result.
TW-041.rightMeaning: A group of related projects managed together to gain benefits you would not get by running them separately.
TW-041.leftScenarioCue: You see this when a team is asked to build one new mobile banking app by December.
TW-041.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the app, a new call center and branch staff training are coordinated together to improve customer experience.
TW-041.trap: A program is not a very large project. Look for several related projects coordinated to deliver benefits together.

TW-042.old: Coordinates related projects and activities to realize combined benefits.
TW-042.hook: Are the pieces related for benefits, or grouped to serve strategy?
TW-042.leftMeaning: Related projects coordinated together to deliver combined benefits.
TW-042.rightMeaning: A collection of projects, programs and other work chosen and ranked to meet company strategy. The pieces need not be related.
TW-042.leftScenarioCue: You see this when three linked projects, a new plant, its supply chain and staff hiring, are managed together to open one factory.
TW-042.rightScenarioCue: You see this when executives rank a factory, a marketing campaign and an IT upgrade to decide which ones get funding this year.
TW-042.rightMemory: Portfolio = strategy, pieces need not relate.
TW-042.trap: Unrelated initiatives being prioritized or funded means portfolio. Portfolio choices follow strategy, not how similar the work is.

TW-043.old: A restriction or limitation that narrows available options, such as budget, deadline, regulation, or resource limits.
TW-043.hook: Is it a limit we must work within, or something we believe?
TW-043.leftMeaning: A limit the team must work within, such as a fixed budget, a deadline, a law or limited staff.
TW-043.rightMeaning: Something the team treats as true for planning, without proof yet.
TW-043.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the contract says the store must open by November 1 and the budget cannot go above $500K.
TW-043.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the PM plans the schedule believing the city permit will arrive within two weeks, though nobody has confirmed it.
TW-043.trap: An assumption is not a fact. Record it in the assumption log and check it again, because a false assumption becomes a risk.
TW-043.memory: CONSTRAINT = limits us. ASSUMPTION = we believe it for planning.

TW-044.old: Raw project observations or measurements without interpretation.
TW-044.hook: Is it a raw number, or a number that has been explained?
TW-044.leftMeaning: Raw facts and measurements, with no meaning added yet.
TW-044.rightMeaning: Data that has been organized and analyzed so people can understand it and make decisions.
TW-044.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the tester logs 42 defects found this week and the hours each team member worked.
TW-044.rightScenarioCue: You see this when the PM's report shows defects rose 30 percent since last sprint, mostly in the payment module.
TW-044.trap: More data does not mean better decisions. Stakeholders need information, so analyze the numbers before you report them.

TW-045.old: A product, service, result, or component produced by the project.
TW-045.hook: Is it the thing we produced, or the benefit it brings?
TW-045.leftMeaning: The product, service or result the project produces.
TW-045.rightMeaning: The real benefit the business or its customers get from using what was delivered.
TW-045.leftScenarioCue: You see this when the team finishes and hands over a new online ordering system, on time and accepted.
TW-045.rightScenarioCue: You see this when customers start ordering online, wait times drop and sales rise by 15 percent.
TW-045.trap: Finishing the deliverable is not the goal. If nobody uses it or benefits never arrive, the project has not delivered value.
